5. The original `Woof._piece` retries takes that have long silences or runaway length. Say how that can work with streaming (e.g. you cannot retry after audio is already playing) and propose a practical rule.
6. Check intelligibility: transcribe the streamed outputs with Whistle (`import cactus; cactus.transcribe(x)["text"]`, x = 16 kHz mono float32 numpy; resample from 24 kHz with numpy interpolation) and report word error rate against the input text for both streamed and non-streamed audio.

8. Save a few WAV samples (streamed Woof juno/mira, Pocket 18m) under `S\expC\samples\` so the owner can listen.

15	
16	# Underdog Woof
17	
18	![Underdog Woof beats models 1,000x its size: download size against word error rate on Gradium TTS Hard Cases, with both Woof models on the Pareto frontier ahead of Fish Audio Drama 3, Phonon, Kokoro, Pocket TTS, Supertonic 3, Kitten Nano, Qwen3-TTS and Liquid AI LFM3-Audio-2B](assets/woof-frontier.png)
19	
20	- **1,022x smaller than Fish Audio Drama 3** (41.5 GB), with **25% fewer word errors**
21	- **1.42% word error rate** on [Gradium TTS Hard Cases](https://huggingface.co/datasets/gradium/tts-hard-sentences-202610) (English, Mira)
22	- **13.8x faster than real time on one CPU thread** (Juno), with no GPU, server or API key
23	- **40.6 MB** for the whole model, both voices included, and 402 MB of memory at peak while it runs (Juno)
24	
25	Underdog Woof is a small English text-to-speech model with two voices: Juno and Mira. It reads phone numbers, dates,
26	prices and codes the way people say them, and it runs on a laptop CPU with nothing but numpy, from a single 40.6 MB
27	file. Try it in your browser at [underdog.ai/woof](https://underdog.ai/woof).
28	
29	## Listen
30	
31	Each voice reads "Please call me back at 415-555-0199 before 5:30 p.m. on Friday." (seed 1).
32	
33	| Voice | |
34	|---|---|
35	| Juno (default) | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof/resolve/main/samples/juno_1.wav"></audio> |
36	| Mira | <audio controls src="https://huggingface.co/ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof/resolve/main/samples/mira_1.wav"></audio> |
37	
38	More clips are in the `samples` folder, listed below.
39	
40	## One voice or two
41	
42	Woof comes in two sizes. This repo is the two-voice model. The one-voice model is the one that runs in your browser at
43	[underdog.ai/woof](https://underdog.ai/woof).
44	
45	| | One voice | Two voices (this repo) |
46	|---|---|---|
47	| Download | 31.7 MB | 40.6 MB |
48	| Peak memory, one CPU thread | 852 MB | 402 MB (Juno) |
49	| Word error rate, Gradium TTS Hard Cases (English) | 2.06% | 1.42% (Mira) |
50	| Speed on one Apple M5 Max CPU thread | 18x real time | 13.8x real time (Juno) |
51	
52	The one-voice speed is plain PyTorch with its int8 weights at the default 16 steps; the two-voice speed is this repo's
53	numpy runtime. Fish Audio Drama 3, for scale, is a 41.5 GB download and gets 1.89% wrong.
54	
55	## How Woof compares
56	
57	Word error rate on Gradium TTS Hard Cases (English, 500 sentences), every model run and scored by us the same way, each
58	in its best-scoring voice. Lower is better.
59	
60	| Model | Runs | Download | Word error rate | Woof's errors are lower by |
61	|---|---|---|---|---|
62	| **Underdog Woof, two voices (Mira)** | **your CPU** | **40.6 MB** | **1.42%** | |
63	| Fish Audio Drama 3 | cloud API | 41.5 GB open weights | 1.89% | 25% |
64	| Underdog Woof, one voice | your CPU or browser | 31.7 MB | 2.06% | |
65	| Phonon 31m | on device | 55.1 MB | 2.16% | 34% |
66	| Deepgram Flux TTS | cloud API | not public | 2.39% | 41% |
67	| Deepgram Aura-2 | cloud API | not public | 2.43% | 42% |
68	| Microsoft MAI-Voice-2.1 Flash | cloud API | not public | 2.51% | 43% |
69	| Fish Audio S2.1 Pro | cloud API | not public | 2.53% | 44% |
70	| Microsoft MAI-Voice-2.1 | cloud API | not public | 2.64% | 46% |
71	| Qwen Audio 3.0 TTS Plus | cloud API | not public | 2.74% | 48% |
72	| Mistral Voxtral 3 TTS | cloud API | not public | 2.91% | 51% |
73	| MiniMax Speech 2.8 Turbo | cloud API | not public | 4.63% | 69% |
74	| MiniMax Speech 2.8 HD | cloud API | not public | 4.88% | 71% |
75	| Kokoro 82M | on device | 327 MB | 5.17% | 73% |
76	| ByteDance Seed Audio 1.0 | cloud API | not public | 6.50% | 78% |
77	| ElevenLabs Flash v2.5 | cloud API | not public | 6.63% | 79% |
78	| Pocket TTS | on device | 219 MB | 8.07% | 82% |
79	| Supertonic 3 | on device | 398 MB | 8.81% | 84% |
80	| Kitten Nano 0.8 | on device | 27.6 MB | 9.81% | 86% |
81	| Qwen3-TTS 1.7B | on device | 4.54 GB | 11.99% | 88% |
82	
83	Kitten Nano 0.8 is the only smaller download, and it gets 9.81% of words wrong: nothing we tested is both smaller and
84	more accurate than Woof. Transcripts by qwen3.8-omni-flash, word errors counted by gemma-4-31b-it. Download is the
85	smallest official set of weights each model needs to run, from its Hugging Face repo in November 2026 (Phonon 31m: the
86	4-bit GGUF; Kitten Nano: the int8 ONNX plus voices; Pocket TTS: the English model; Qwen3-TTS: the model plus its speech
87	tokenizer). Cloud-only models don't publish a size.
88	
89	**Liquid AI LFM3-Audio-2B** (1.21 GB, 4-bit GGUF) gets **20.1%** of words wrong (747 of 3,718) in a separate run of the
90	same 500 sentences. Liquid publishes no word error rate for its speech, and qwen3.8-omni-flash is an API we couldn't use
91	for that run, so its transcripts are by Whisper large-v3, with errors still counted by gemma-4-31b-it. As a check, Kokoro
92	scored 4.29% that way against 5.17% above, so LFM3-Audio-2B's number on the setup above is likely a little higher, not
93	lower. It was run in BF16 with the settings on its model card (an American English female voice, one seed per sentence); 1.21 GB is its smallest official download.
94	
95	![Underdog Woof to scale by download size: 40.6 MB next to Kokoro, VibeVoice 1.5B, Sesame CSM 1B, Orpheus 3B and Fish Audio Drama 3 at 41.5 GB](assets/woof-to-scale.png)
96	
97	## Results by voice
98	
99	All numbers are for the files in this repo, run exactly as `python -m underdog_woof` runs them.
100	
101	| | Juno | Mira |
102	|---|---|---|
103	| Word error rate, Gradium TTS Hard Cases (English) | 1.53% | 1.42% |
104	| Word errors | 67 in 4,371 | 62 in 4,379 |
105	| Speed on one Apple M5 Max CPU thread | 13.8x real time | 7.2x real time |
106	| Peak resident memory | 402 MB | 601 MB |
107	
108	Speed is the median of three rounds over 200 everyday sentences on one CPU thread of an Apple M5 Max.
109	
110	## Usage
111	
112	```bash
113	pip install numpy
114	hf download ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof --local-dir underdog-woof
115	cd underdog-woof
116	python -m underdog_woof "Your order ships on March 3rd. Call 415-555-0199 with questions." -o hello.wav
117	python -m underdog_woof "Your order ships on March 3rd. Call 415-555-0199 with questions." --voice mira -o mira.wav
118	```
119	
120	```python
121	from underdog_woof import Woof
122	
123	tts = Woof(voice="mira")   # "juno" (default) or "mira"
124	audio = tts("Hey! Thanks for calling. How can I help you today?", seed=0)   # float32 mono, 24 kHz
125	tts.save("hello.wav", audio)
126	```
127	
128	Give Woof the text as you would write it. A built-in rule-based normalizer rewrites numbers, dates, times, money,
129	codes and symbols the way people say them, and respells hard names from a lexicon. It needs nothing beyond the
130	standard library. Pass `normalize=False` to `Woof()` if you'd rather do this yourself.
131	
132	Long text is split into sentences, and a sentence over 120 characters is split again at its commas, semicolons or
133	dashes. Each piece is checked as it's made. If it runs far too long for its text or has a second or more of silence in
134	the middle, Woof draws it again, up to three more times, and keeps the best take. The results above were measured with
135	these settings, one seed per sentence. Pass a `seed` to get the same audio for the same text every time.
136	
137	## Samples
138	
139	The `samples` folder has three clips per voice, each made with the seed shown:
140	
141	- `juno_0.wav`, `mira_0.wav` (seed 0): "Your order ships on March 3rd, and the tracking code is QX-4471."

143	- `juno_2.wav`, `mira_2.wav` (seed 2): "The committee, which had met every Tuesday since the spring of
144	  2019, finally agreed that the budget would need a second review before anyone could sign it, and that the review
145	  should be public."

# WoofVoice

Streams (or outputs) speech from a local Underdog Woof TTS model in response to OpenAI-compatible, Ollama, or Anthropic requests.

Features include:

- Streaming audio output, with optional chunked output for external players
- Multiple providers and models, including OpenAI, Ollama, and Anthropic
- Multiple voices (powered by Underdog Woof), including Mira and Juno
- Routing audio to virtual devices like VB-CABLE
- In-process notifications when each audio chunk is ready
- Both command-line usage and library usage

## Setup

First, clone this repository.

It's recommended to use a virtual environment, like `uv` but you can also manually set it up.

### UV

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), then run:

```bash
uv sync
source .venv/bin/activate
hf download ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof --local-dir underdog-woof
```

### Manual

1. Install dependencies:

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

2. Download the Underdog Woof model:

```bash
hf download ConwayResearch/Underdog-Woof --local-dir underdog-woof
```

If you don't have `hf` installed, you can install it with:

```bash
pip install hf
```

## Usage

Set the provider settings in `.env`, then run:

```bash
woofvoice "Tell me a short joke." --output response.wav
```

(or `python main.py "Tell me a short joke." --output response.wav` if you don't have the script installed)

Select a provider explicitly when needed:

```bash
woofvoice --provider ollama --model llama3.2 "Tell me a short joke."
woofvoice --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-5 "Tell me a short joke."
```

Use `--voice mira` to select the Mira voice, or `--no-play` to save audio without playing it.

To route live audio to VB-CABLE or another virtual device, list available outputs:

```bash
woofvoice --list-audio-devices
woofvoice --audio-device "VB-CABLE" "Tell me a short joke."
```

You can also set `AUDIO_DEVICE` in `.env`. Use the device name or numeric index shown by
`--list-audio-devices`; the WAV file is still saved normally.

To expose each spoken segment as soon as it is generated, write chunks to a directory:

```bash
woofvoice --chunk-dir ./audio-chunks "Tell me a short joke."
```

Each file is a complete WAV named with a unique run ID, sequence number, and text hash,
for example `a1b2c3d4e5f6-000001-9f2a1c4d8e77.wav`. An external player can watch this
directory and play files in sequence. Files are written atomically, so only complete
audio files appear with the `.wav` extension. The same option is available through
`AUDIO_CHUNK_DIR` in `.env` and as `chunk_dir` in `stream_and_speak()`.

For in-process notifications, pass `on_chunk`. It receives an `AudioChunkEvent`
after the file is ready, including `run_id`, `index`, `text`, and `path`:

```python
from woofvoice import AudioChunkEvent

def new_chunk(event: AudioChunkEvent) -> None:
    print(f"Play section {event.index}: {event.text} ({event.path})")

stream_and_speak(tokens, tts, "response.wav", chunk_dir="audio-chunks", on_chunk=new_chunk)
```

## Use as a library

```python
from underdog_woof import Woof
from woofvoice import OllamaChatBackend, stream_and_speak

backend = OllamaChatBackend("http://localhost:11434", "llama3.2")
stream_and_speak(
    backend.stream([{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]),
    Woof(voice="juno"),
    "response.wav",
    audio_device="VB-CABLE",
    chunk_dir="audio-chunks",
)
```

## License

This project is licensed under the MIT License. See the [LICENSE](LICENSE) file for details.

**License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. Non-commercial use, sharing, and adaptation are permitted with credit to Underdog. Commercial use requires a separate license from license@conway.tech. Upstream components keep their original licenses, including Apache for some files.

**Not covered on this page:** The page does not include the prompts, base model name, relationship to the selector or main woof models, training details, latency figures, or code beyond the install and server commands. Those would need to come from the full model card or the repository files.

The article doesn't cover most of what you asked. It has no details on Underdog's assistant architecture, the roles of any small models (filler, selector, or PII), the voice pipeline, or how Woof was built. It also gives no roadmap. Here is what it does say:

**Woof (voice model)**
- A text-to-speech model that the article calls "frontier." The tweet it quotes gives its size as 31.7 MB, and the headline rounds to 32 MB.
- It has 31 million parameters and is open for anyone to download.
- The company says it runs on most devices without an internet connection, and the demo runs in a browser.

**Demo game**
- A retro room with a typewriter, CRT monitor, desk lamp, and music tuner.
- Typed text is spoken back, and rotating the tuner generates different kinds of music.
- The article notes that all voices in the game are Woof.

**Other models**
- Bark: a 167 MB speech-to-text model for on-device transcription and dictation, launched weeks before the demo.
- An unnamed 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops.

**Company direction**
- Founder Sigil Wen says he started the app because he wanted his own notetaking system, rather than tools like Granola, built on models that run on users' devices.
- He said: "I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months."
- The company's stated goal is to "allow people to have private AI."
- A waitlisted app is positioned as a locally hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

For the architecture, pipeline, and roadmap details, you would need Underdog's own documentation, such as its manifesto or model release pages.

content:
I like the current speculative reflex cascade direction. Continue with the existing experiments, but I want you to consider some additional research directions before finalizing the architecture.

Investigate true full-duplex conversation, including barge-in, acoustic echo cancellation, backchannels, interruption handling, cancellation, overlapping speech and false interruptions. I don't want this to become just a fast traditional voice pipeline.

Explore aggressive speculative execution, where STT, intent prediction, data retrieval, reasoning and speech preparation can begin before the user finishes speaking. Investigate how speculative work can be cancelled or reused safely. Never execute financial writes speculatively.

For the router, also benchmark classical lightweight approaches such as TF-IDF, logistic regression, rule-based classifiers and tiny neural networks. Don't assume we need a generative LLM for every component.

Investigate pre-generated audio responses and speculative TTS preparation as another way to reduce perceived latency without making the conversation repetitive or unnatural.



btw all these points fully extra up to you how u want to proceed i just want you to have a fully open view and full testing so the final thing is actually amazing
