tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Check an HTML page before html_render. Returns PNG, contentHeight, and console output. Self-contained: inline <style> and <script>. Local images as absolute paths are inlined. Remote URLs load as-is. Theme and layout rules are in html_render.

path.description: Absolute .html file path.

width.description: CSS pixels, 240 to 1600. Default 728. Use about 390 for phones.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, diagram, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final reply. Do not announce or restate the page. Frame fits height to 20000px. On mobile, content past the given height scrolls. Frame width is reply width (728px desktop, about 360px phones), on the thread background. Leave html, body, and the outer element with no background color, no outer card, border, banner title, or side padding. This wins over any rule that sets a page background. T3 adds an overridable 8px html gutter for selection rings and shadows. Use fluid widths within it. A box that needs its own background gets 16px padding and var(--radius) corners. Give charts fixed pixel heights. Let content set the height. Do not use vh units or height:100% on html or body. Both are rejected or loop. Use theme CSS variables on :root, not fixed colors: --background, --foreground, --muted, --card, --popover, --secondary, --border, --ring, --primary, --accent, --destructive, --warning, --success, --info, --code-background (most have a matching -foreground; accent, destructive, and warning also have -surface), --chart-1 to --chart-6, --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base sheet sets background, text, and font.

path.description: Absolute .html file path.

height.description: Frame height in CSS pixels, 80 to 2000. Use the contentHeight from html_preview.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__request_secret
tools.description: Ask for one secret per single-line card; never combine values. Open it, don't offer it. Returns one-use `secretRef`, or `delivery: "file"` a file read only in its command, e.g. `adb pair <ip:port> "$(cat <file>)"`. Asked how: call now. Sign-in link: `url`. Pasted secret for child/script: `value`. Never from an old thread.

url.description: Sign-in or setup page for the value. Shown as a button.

delivery.description: secretRef (default) for a T3 tool; file for a command.

value.description: Pasted in this thread; no card.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__send_to_user
tools.description: Show the user a Markdown message in this thread, exactly as written, before your turn ends. Use it for content the user must read in full mid-turn, such as a draft, a code block, or what a question you are about to ask refers to. Don't repeat it in your reply.

lastPrompt: Continue where you left off.

input.prompt:
You are running one research experiment for a voice-agent project. Do the work yourself; do not start subagents. Do NOT touch any git repository, and do not write outside the scratchpad directory below (except pip/HF caches). Do not use Ollama.

## Context
We are designing a self-hosted, modular, **true full-duplex** voice call pipeline for a personal-finance app (English first) that should beat OpenAI's realtime voice. It is a cascade of tiny CPU models: Cactus Whistle speech-to-text (16.9 MB, ~100 ms for a 4 s clip, has a streaming mode), a turn detector, a tiny router, and a streaming TTS (Kyutai Pocket TTS, ~80 ms to first audio). The owner does not want "just a fast turn-based pipeline": the assistant must keep listening while it speaks, stop when the user really interrupts, NOT stop for a "mm-hm", a cough, or its own voice coming back through the speakers, and resume gracefully after a false alarm. Client is a browser (which offers WebRTC echo cancellation via getUserMedia), server runs on the same laptop; but laptop speakers + open mic leak echo, and we want a second line of defence on the server.

Your experiment: **barge-in, echo and backchannel handling while the assistant is speaking**, simulated offline with real models.

### Ideas to test
1. **Acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) as line one.** Find an AEC that runs in Python on Windows x64 (candidates: `livekit` rtc `AudioProcessingModule` (WebRTC APM: AEC3, noise suppression), `speexdsp`/`pyaec`, `webrtc-audio-processing` bindings, or a small neural AEC with ONNX). Simulate the mic signal as: user speech + (assistant TTS audio convolved with a synthetic room impulse response, delayed 40-120 ms, at several echo levels, e.g. echo-to-user ratios of -20, -10, 0, +6 dB) + light noise. Measure echo return loss enhancement and residual.
2. **Transcript-level self-speech filter as line two (our own idea, please test it properly).** The server knows exactly which text the TTS is speaking and when. Run Whistle on the mic signal during playback; if the recognised words are (fuzzily) a subsequence of the words currently being played, it is echo, not the user. Words that are not explained by the playing text are user speech. Measure how well this separates "echo only" from "echo + user speaking over it", with and without AEC in front. Consider alignment by word timestamps (`cactus.transcribe(x, word_timestamps=True)` returns words with start/end/probability) against the known TTS schedule.
3. **Barge-in policy.** A staged policy like: voice activity on the cleaned mic for 150 ms -> duck playback volume (reversible); confirmed as real user words (not echo, not a backchannel) -> stop TTS and cancel; short backchannel ("mm-hm", "yeah", "okay", "right", a cough) -> restore volume and continue the same sentence. Compare (a) plain VAD-triggered stop (what naive pipelines do), (b) AEC + VAD, (c) AEC + VAD + self-speech filter + backchannel lexicon/duration rule. Use Silero VAD (ONNX, pip `silero-vad` or the onnx file) or an energy VAD.
4. Measure for each policy over a set of at least 60 simulated events (about one third each: echo only/no user speech; user backchannel over assistant speech; real interruption over assistant speech such as "no wait, I meant last month" or "stop, how much was rent?"):
   - false-stop rate on echo-only and on backchannels (lower is better)
   - miss rate on real interruptions
   - time from the start of the user's interrupting speech to (i) duck and (ii) confirmed stop
   - Whistle word error rate on the user's interrupting utterance (transcribed from the mic during overlap), with and without AEC, since the interruption text is what the agent must answer next.
5. Also report what context must be recorded when a stop happens: how to compute which words of the assistant's sentence were actually heard by the user before the cut (from the TTS chunk schedule), so the conversation history contains only what was really played.

## Setup on disk
- Scratchpad root S = `C:\Users\mgsuk\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ccf816f539b7556e\84c9502f-eb89-46cc-b4c6-818cd19ea24b\scratchpad`. Put all your files under `S\expD\`.
- Create your own venv (`python -m venv S\expD\venv`, Python 3.11, Windows 11, i5-12450HX 8 cores, 16 GB RAM) and install what you need: `cactus-compute numpy soundfile scipy onnxruntime pocket-tts` etc.
- Whistle: `import cactus; cactus.transcribe(x, language="en", keywords=[...], word_timestamps=True)` where x is a WAV path or 16 kHz mono float32 numpy in [-1,1]; `cactus.stream(chunks)` for live partials (read the docstrings with inspect). First use downloads the weights.
- Pocket TTS to synthesize both the assistant's speech and the simulated user's speech (use clearly different voices, e.g. assistant "alba", user "marius" or "javert"): `from pocket_tts import TTSModel; m = TTSModel.load_model(language="english_18m_2026-10"); st = m.get_state_for_audio_prompt("alba"); chunks = list(m.generate_audio_stream(st, text))` (torch tensors at `m.sample_rate`, 24 kHz; resample to 16 kHz with scipy for the mic path). Voice names available: cosette, marius, javert, alba, jean, anna, vera, fantine, charles, paul, eponine, azelma, george, mary, jane, michael, eve.
- Env: `CACTUS_TELEMETRY=0`, `HF_HUB_DISABLE_SYMLINKS_WARNING=1`, `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8`. Python's open() defaults to cp1252 here: always pass `encoding="utf-8"`.
- Assistant sentences should be finance-call style ("You spent 312 euros on groceries in October, about 18 percent more than September, and most of it was at Rewe and Netto."), long enough (5-8 s) to interrupt at random points.

Limits to be honest about: synthetic voices and a synthetic room are easier than a real laptop; say so, and say which results you expect to transfer. Other experiments share this CPU, so timing may be noisy; use medians.

Time-box about 90 minutes of wall time. If no AEC library installs on Windows, say exactly what failed, implement a simple NLMS/frequency-domain adaptive filter in numpy as the fallback, and continue.

## Report back (final message, plain text)
- What AEC you used and how much echo it removed at each level.
- Results table per policy: false stops on echo, false stops on backchannels, missed interruptions, median/p95 time to duck and to stop, WER of the interruption.
- Whether the transcript-level self-speech filter works, where it fails, and its cost in ms.
- A recommended barge-in state machine (states, thresholds, timers) based on your numbers.
- What you could not verify offline and would need a real microphone/speaker test.
- Paths: scripts, a few example WAVs (`S\expD\samples\`), and `S\expD\results.json`.
Do not overstate; report failures plainly.

The search turned up a handful of relevant sources, though most are vendor blogs or preprints rather than peer-reviewed studies.

**Benchmarks**
- Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 is the most direct match for your query. It tests user interruptions and backchannels as separate capabilities, using synthesized speech from the same speaker. Its backchannel test checks whether a model ignores cues like "yeah" or "mm-hmm" ([arxiv 2507.23159](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23159)).
- Full-Duplex-Bench v3 covers tool use under real-world disfluency ([arxiv 2604.04847](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.04847)). EVA-Bench is a 2026 end-to-end voice-agent evaluation framework ([arxiv 2605.13841](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.13841)). MTR-DuplexBench covers multi-round evaluation ([arxiv 2511.10262](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.10262)).

**False interruptions and echo**
- A practitioner guide cites a 2022 Alibaba study. It reports that under a simple ASR-confidence rule, 89% of barge-in events were false interruptions ([Roark](https://roark.ai/blog/testing-full-duplex-voice-agents)). I could not verify that figure against the original paper.
- Echo is a common cause of false yields. Leaked agent audio can trigger VAD, so the agent interrupts itself. Acoustic echo cancellation is therefore treated as a requirement for full-duplex agents ([Soniox](https://soniox.com/wiki/turn-taking-barge-in)).
- LiveKit treats a VAD trigger with an empty transcript as a false interruption and can resume speech where it stopped ([Duplex Compute](https://duplexcompute.com/research/full-duplex-voice-ai/)).

**Cascaded versus native full-duplex**
- A cascaded agent with VAD can stop when the caller speaks, but it does not handle backchannels. Several sources say that gap is what native full-duplex models are meant to close ([EvalGent](https://www.evalgent.com/blog/full-duplex-voice-agents)).
- Recent architecture work includes a plug-in streaming state-prediction module ([SoulX-Duplug, arxiv 2603.14877](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.14877)) and a playback-aligned context engine ([PACE, arxiv 2608.07631](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.07631)).

**Caveat:** Roark's suggested test scenarios are a practitioner checklist, not a published benchmark. I did not find a 2026 paper that jointly measures barge-in, backchannel, and echo handling for cascaded pipelines. That gap may be worth a follow-up search.

content.content:
**What it is:** DFlash here is a speculative-decoding draft model, an inference technique rather than a standalone model. The card says it "is not a standalone language model." It runs next to Underdog Poodle 4B, proposes tokens, and Poodle verifies them.

**How it speeds generation:** The draft proposes up to 15 tokens at a time, and Poodle checks them in a single forward pass. Poodle accepts or rejects each token, so its output distribution stays the same as without the draft. The draft reads Poodle's hidden states from selected layers and fills a block of masked positions in one pass.

**Speedups (single request, one H100 80GB, vLLM 0.31):**
- Agent episodes with tools: 210 to 462 tokens/s (2.2x)
- BFCL tool calls: 213 to 621 (2.9x)
- IFEval: 222 to 451 (2.0x)
- GSM8K: 222 to 677 (3.0x)
- HumanEval: 222 to 925 (4.2x)
- MT-Bench: 222 to 395 (1.8x)

Against the Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash draft, this draft runs 32% to 36% faster on tool calls and agent turns. With 32 concurrent requests, the card suggests using 7 drafted tokens instead of 15.

**How to run:** Serve Poodle with vLLM 0.31 or newer and pass a speculative config that sets the method to dflash, points to this draft model, and sets `num_speculative_tokens` to 15 (or 7 for many concurrent requests). The card also lists tool-call and reasoning parser flags.

**Pairs with:** Underdog Poodle 4B (ConwayResearch/Underdog-Poodle-4B), which it drafts for.

**Hardware:** Benchmarks were run on one H100 80GB. The draft itself is about 634M parameters in bf16, with six decoder layers and no embedding or output head of its own.

**License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. Non-commercial use, sharing, and adaptation are allowed with credit to Underdog. Commercial use requires a separate license from license@conway.tech. It is built on Qwen3.5-4B and z-lab's Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash, both Apache 2.0.

content.content:
**Underdog Bark 3.0** is an English-only speech recognition model from ConwayResearch, fine-tuned from NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3.

- **Size and parameters:** The card describes it as "a 0.6B English model in a 163 MB download." It is the smallest member of the family that has the same accuracy as the larger members.
- **Languages:** English only.
- **Streaming:** The card doesn't say whether the model supports streaming. It describes whole-file transcription, and notes that long recordings should be split into pieces of a few minutes on 8 or 16 GB Macs.
- **Accuracy:** It averages 4.94% word error rate across seven English Open ASR Leaderboard sets. Comparisons on the same averaged metric:
  - Parakeet TDT 0.6B v3: 4.94%, at 2,508 MB
  - Phonon-2: 5.21%, at 164 MB
  - Qwen3-ASR-0.6B: 5.16%, at 1,876 MB
  - Whisper large-v3: 6.04%, at 9,261 MB

  The Bark rows were scored with the leaderboard's code but aren't on the leaderboard yet.
- **Speed:** On an Apple M2 laptop with stock mlx-audio, a minute of audio takes about 1.5 seconds, which the card gives as "41x realtime."
- **Windows (CPU):** Use 64-bit Python 3.11 in a new virtual environment. Install the CPU build of torch 2.8.0 from PyTorch's CPU index, then the Windows requirements file. Run `transcribe_bark.py` with `--device cpu`. The loader expands the weights to FP32 in memory, so RAM needs exceed the 163 MB download. The card says CUDA was tested on Windows, but it doesn't say the CPU path was.
- **License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. The card lists license@conway.tech as the contact for commercial use.
- **Variants:**
  - **Bark 3.0:** 163 MB, 4.94% average. The base model.
  - **Bark 3.0 Plus:** 180 MB, 4.76% average.
  - **Bark 3.0 Pro:** 1,254 MB, 4.29% average, full precision.
  - **Bark 3.0 Clean:** Removes filler words like "um." The card links to it but gives no benchmark for it.

Web search results for query: "full-duplex voice agent barge-in false interruption backchannel detection research 2026 echo cancellation cascaded pipeline interruption handling benchmark"

Links: [{"title":"A frontend-backend architecture for tool calls in full-duplex speech models","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.19334"},{"title":"Testing full-duplex voice agents: what breaks when the pipeline collapses into one model - Roark","url":"https://roark.ai/blog/testing-full-duplex-voice-agents"},{"title":"PACE: A Playback-Aligned Context Engine for LLM-Based Full-Duplex Voice Dialogue","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.07631"},{"title":"Full-Duplex Voice Agents: Simultaneous Speech (2026)","url":"https://www.evalgent.com/blog/full-duplex-voice-agents"},{"title":"Turn-taking and barge-in: how voice agents know when to talk","url":"https://soniox.com/wiki/turn-taking-barge-in"},{"title":"MP-Bench: Evaluating Voice Agents as a Multiparty Conversation Participant","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.13076"},{"title":"SoulX-Duplug: Plug-and-Play Streaming State Prediction Module for Realtime Full-Duplex Speech Conversation","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.14877"},{"title":"Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5: Evaluating Overlap Handling for Full-Duplex Speech Models","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23159"},{"title":"Full-duplex voice AI vs. turn-based: barge-in and overlap — Duplex Compute","url":"https://duplexcompute.com/research/full-duplex-voice-ai/"}]

The search turned up a handful of relevant sources, though most are vendor blogs or preprints rather than peer-reviewed studies.

**Benchmarks**
- Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 is the most direct match for your query. It tests user interruptions and backchannels as separate capabilities, using synthesized speech from the same speaker. Its backchannel test checks whether a model ignores cues like "yeah" or "mm-hmm" ([arxiv 2507.23159](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.23159)).
- Full-Duplex-Bench v3 covers tool use under real-world disfluency ([arxiv 2604.04847](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.04847)). EVA-Bench is a 2026 end-to-end voice-agent evaluation framework ([arxiv 2605.13841](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.13841)). MTR-DuplexBench covers multi-round evaluation ([arxiv 2511.10262](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.10262)).

**False interruptions and echo**
- A practitioner guide cites a 2022 Alibaba study. It reports that under a simple ASR-confidence rule, 89% of barge-in events were false interruptions ([Roark](https://roark.ai/blog/testing-full-duplex-voice-agents)). I could not verify that figure against the original paper.
- Echo is a common cause of false yields. Leaked agent audio can trigger VAD, so the agent interrupts itself. Acoustic echo cancellation is therefore treated as a requirement for full-duplex agents ([Soniox](https://soniox.com/wiki/turn-taking-barge-in)).
- LiveKit treats a VAD trigger with an empty transcript as a false interruption and can resume speech where it stopped ([Duplex Compute](https://duplexcompute.com/research/full-duplex-voice-ai/)).

**Cascaded versus native full-duplex**
- A cascaded agent with VAD can stop when the caller speaks, but it does not handle backchannels. Several sources say that gap is what native full-duplex models are meant to close ([EvalGent](https://www.evalgent.com/blog/full-duplex-voice-agents)).
- Recent architecture work includes a plug-in streaming state-prediction module ([SoulX-Duplug, arxiv 2603.14877](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.14877)) and a playback-aligned context engine ([PACE, arxiv 2608.07631](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.07631)).

**Caveat:** Roark's suggested test scenarios are a practitioner checklist, not a published benchmark. I did not find a 2026 paper that jointly measures barge-in, backchannel, and echo handling for cascaded pipelines. That gap may be worth a follow-up search.

- **Community:** 1 like, 201 downloads last month.
- **License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. Non-commercial use is permitted with credit to Underdog. Commercial use requires a separate license from license@conway.tech. Upstream components keep their own licenses (Apache 2.0 file referenced).

**What it is:** DFlash here is a speculative-decoding draft model, an inference technique rather than a standalone model. The card says it "is not a standalone language model." It runs next to Underdog Poodle 4B, proposes tokens, and Poodle verifies them.

**How it speeds generation:** The draft proposes up to 15 tokens at a time, and Poodle checks them in a single forward pass. Poodle accepts or rejects each token, so its output distribution stays the same as without the draft. The draft reads Poodle's hidden states from selected layers and fills a block of masked positions in one pass.

**Speedups (single request, one H100 80GB, vLLM 0.31):**
- Agent episodes with tools: 210 to 462 tokens/s (2.2x)
- BFCL tool calls: 213 to 621 (2.9x)
- IFEval: 222 to 451 (2.0x)
- GSM8K: 222 to 677 (3.0x)
- HumanEval: 222 to 925 (4.2x)
- MT-Bench: 222 to 395 (1.8x)

Against the Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash draft, this draft runs 32% to 36% faster on tool calls and agent turns. With 32 concurrent requests, the card suggests using 7 drafted tokens instead of 15.

**How to run:** Serve Poodle with vLLM 0.31 or newer and pass a speculative config that sets the method to dflash, points to this draft model, and sets `num_speculative_tokens` to 15 (or 7 for many concurrent requests). The card also lists tool-call and reasoning parser flags.

**Pairs with:** Underdog Poodle 4B (ConwayResearch/Underdog-Poodle-4B), which it drafts for.

**Hardware:** Benchmarks were run on one H100 80GB. The draft itself is about 634M parameters in bf16, with six decoder layers and no embedding or output head of its own.

**License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. Non-commercial use, sharing, and adaptation are allowed with credit to Underdog. Commercial use requires a separate license from license@conway.tech. It is built on Qwen3.5-4B and z-lab's Qwen3.5-4B-DFlash, both Apache 2.0.

**Underdog Bark 3.0** is an English-only speech recognition model from ConwayResearch, fine-tuned from NVIDIA's parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3.

- **Size and parameters:** The card describes it as "a 0.6B English model in a 163 MB download." It is the smallest member of the family that has the same accuracy as the larger members.
- **Languages:** English only.
- **Streaming:** The card doesn't say whether the model supports streaming. It describes whole-file transcription, and notes that long recordings should be split into pieces of a few minutes on 8 or 16 GB Macs.
- **Accuracy:** It averages 4.94% word error rate across seven English Open ASR Leaderboard sets. Comparisons on the same averaged metric:

  - Phonon-2: 5.21%, at 164 MB
  - Qwen3-ASR-0.6B: 5.16%, at 1,876 MB
  - Whisper large-v3: 6.04%, at 9,261 MB

  The Bark rows were scored with the leaderboard's code but aren't on the leaderboard yet.

- **Windows (CPU):** Use 64-bit Python 3.11 in a new virtual environment. Install the CPU build of torch 2.8.0 from PyTorch's CPU index, then the Windows requirements file. Run `transcribe_bark.py` with `--device cpu`. The loader expands the weights to FP32 in memory, so RAM needs exceed the 163 MB download. The card says CUDA was tested on Windows, but it doesn't say the CPU path was.
- **License:** CC BY-NC 4.0. The card lists license@conway.tech as the contact for commercial use.
- **Variants:**

  - **Bark 3.0 Plus:** 180 MB, 4.76% average.

content.thinking:
I'm weighing whether to resume the agents one at a time or finish the experiments myself, since their saved contexts are expensive to reload. The limit resets at 1am and it's 1am now, so the cost of each option matters.

Experiment B's results are mostly done, so I can summarize them with a small script. For A, the costly embeddings already exist and train_heads.py is ready to run. C is partly benchmarked, and D has its corpus but no simulation script yet. I'll run the existing scripts myself and read the outputs compactly, starting with a summary of B's results.json keys.

content.content:
"""Train small end-of-turn heads on frozen Whistle encoder frames and evaluate on the official test split.

Usage: python train_heads.py [--epochs 25] [--only name1,name2]
Reads expA/emb/{train,test}_*.npz, writes expA/heads/<name>.pt, expA/head_probs.npz and expA/train_results.json.
"""
import argparse
import glob
import json
import os
import time

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
DIM = 512
T = 63  # last 5 s of 80 ms frames (Whistle.embed gets ~7x slower above 64 frames)


def load(split):
    frames, lens, y, meta = [], [], [], []
    for p in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(HERE, "emb", f"{split}_*.npz"))):
        z = np.load(p, allow_pickle=False)

"""Score amount fidelity: every number in the sentence must come back exactly after TTS -> Whistle."""
import json, os, sys, wave
import numpy as np
HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)); sys.path.insert(0, HERE)
os.environ.setdefault("CACTUS_TELEMETRY", "0")
import cactus
from textnorm import numbers_recovered
from fidelity_gen import FID

def load16k(path):
    with wave.open(path, "rb") as w:
        sr = w.getframerate(); x = np.frombuffer(w.readframes(w.getnframes()), dtype="<i2").astype(np.float32) / 32768.0
    n = int(len(x) * 16000 / sr)
    return np.interp(np.linspace(0, len(x) - 1, n), np.arange(len(x)), x).astype(np.float32)

out = {}
for folder in sorted(os.listdir(os.path.join(HERE, "audio"))):
    if not folder.startswith("fid_"): continue
    ok = nums_ok = nums_all = 0; fails = []
    for i, (text, nums) in enumerate(FID):
        p = os.path.join(HERE, "audio", folder, f"{i:02d}.wav")
        if not os.path.exists(p): continue
        hyp = cactus.transcribe(load16k(p), language="en")["text"]
        good, found = numbers_recovered(nums, hyp)
        g = sum(bool(x) for x in good) if isinstance(good, (list, tuple)) else int(good)
        allok = (g == len(nums)) if isinstance(good, (list, tuple)) else bool(good)
        ok += allok; nums_ok += g if isinstance(good, (list, tuple)) else (len(nums) if good else 0); nums_all += len(nums)
        if not allok: fails.append({"text": text, "heard": hyp})
    out[folder] = {"sentences_exact": ok, "of": len(FID), "numbers_ok": nums_ok, "numbers": nums_all, "fails": fails}
    print(folder, f"sentences exact {ok}/{len(FID)}", flush=True)
    for f in fails[:6]: print("   ", f["text"], "=>", f["heard"])
json.dump(out, open(os.path.join(HERE, "res_fidelity.json"), "w", encoding="utf-8"), indent=1, ensure_ascii=False)

I'm reviewing the three test setups: raw VAD stops falsely every time, AEC with VAD still falsely stops on echo and backchannels, and adding a filter cuts those false stops but misses some speech and runs slower.

I'm weighing the findings: AEC is clearly necessary, and a text-level self-speech filter sharply cuts false stops, though at the cost of slower stops and some missed speech. The synthetic setup is harsh, since the simulated user is as loud as the echo, so the results may be pessimistic. Transcription during overlap is unreliable, which points toward stopping TTS quickly on barge-in and transcribing the user's speech once playback ends.

I'm working out that ducking playback when VAD fires would lower the echo by roughly 15 dB, which should make the rest of the user's speech cleaner to transcribe and speed up the decision. My simulation left out this effect, so I'm planning to add it as a second pass that reduces the reference signal after the duck point.

I'm now going to add ducking to the simulation: when the VAD fires, playback gets attenuated by about 15 dB, which should reduce the echo and make the user's speech cleaner. I'm also weighing a quicker stop rule that ends playback immediately on interruption cue words like "stop," "wait," or "no," while still waiting for more words when the input is only "okay" or "yeah."

I'm switching the simulation to two passes: the first finds when ducking would trigger, and the second rebuilds the mic signal with playback attenuated from that point, then reruns AEC and the decision logic. I'm also planning to test decision times at 0.3 through 1.8 seconds and add a cue-word list, then patch the script.

# Self-hosted full-duplex voice for Moneo: research log

Goal: a modular, plug-and-play voice call pipeline that we own, English first, that beats OpenAI's GPT-Live for Moneo's use (fast first reaction, real full-duplex behaviour, exact money facts, no per-minute cost). Everything here was run on the dev laptop (i5-12450HX, 16 GB RAM, RTX 3050 6 GB, Windows 11) unless noted.

Scripts and raw results live in the session scratchpad (not in the repo):
`C:\Users\mgsuk\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ccf816f539b7556e\84c9502f-eb89-46cc-b4c6-818cd19ea24b\scratchpad` (`spike\`, `expA\` to `expD\`). Copy them somewhere durable before a reboot if you want to keep them.

Status key: DONE = measured, PARTIAL = measured with known gaps, TODO = not yet run.

## 1. What exists (literature and products)

| System | Kind | What it shows | Why it is not our answer as is |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI GPT-Live (`gpt-live-1`) | Closed speech-to-speech + delegation | About 0.8 s turn-taking latency (read off OpenAI's chart), delegates real work to a backend model | Paid per minute, cloud only, rephrases results, waits for end of turn before delegating |
| NVIDIA NemotronLabs VoiceChat (11B, Sept 2026) | Open full-duplex with tool calls | Best open full-duplex model; 448 ms smooth-turn latency | H100-class GPU, English, tool arguments right only 42%, no barge-in during tools, 2 min audio context |
| Moshi, PersonaPlex (7B) | Open full-duplex | 170-265 ms latency, good interruptions | Weak task quality (VoiceBench about 30), no tools |
| DuplexCascade (Interspeech 2026) | Cascade made full-duplex | Fine-tuning only a text LLM with control tokens (wait / respond / interrupted / backchannel) on 0.6 s micro-turns beats Moshi and PersonaPlex at turn-taking | Needs a 7B LLM in the loop every 0.6 s |
| Voice-Light (arXiv 2609.20995) | Cascade with speculative generation | Private speculative replies promoted after transcript checks: 667 ms vs 1,513 ms median | Two A10 GPUs, English, does not address tool side effects, learned turn head failed (12.5% recall) |
| LTS-VoiceAgent (EMNLP 2026) | "Think while listening" | Semantic trigger starts reasoning on prefixes | No tools, no numbers available to us |
| Talker-Reasoner, ConvFill, Ping-Ponder | Fast talker + slow reasoner | Filler speech hides reasoner latency | Talker is still an LLM |
| Full-Duplex-Bench v1/1.5/3 | Benchmarks | Pause handling, backchannels, interruptions, tool use under disfluency; self-correction is the most common failure everywhere | Use as our evaluation later |

Conclusion: nothing open beats GPT-Live out of the box on a laptop, and fine-tuning a 7-11B full-duplex model is out of reach. The open gap is a cascade of tiny parts that behaves full-duplex and starts the real work early.

## 2. Building blocks measured

### Speech to text: Cactus Whistle (16.9 MB, Apache-2.0) — DONE
- 3-5 s English sentences transcribed in 84-158 ms on CPU, 0 errors on plain questions.
- Streaming mode gives committed words plus a pending tail every 0.5 s chunk (pass 30-900 ms).
- German: 3 of 4 sentences perfect, one word wrong ("in bar" heard as "in Bahn").
- Weak spots: "net worth" heard as "network" (fixable with the `keywords` bias list), inconsistent number formatting ("3,400 and 80").
- `embed()` is not free: 94-162 ms per second of audio when measured while other jobs ran, and it slows a lot above 64 frames. Needs a clean re-measure.
- Alternative: Underdog Bark 3.0 (163 MB, English, 4.94% WER, non-commercial licence). Not tested.

### Text to speech — DONE
| Model | Size | Licence | First sound (CPU) | Speed | Numbers spoken right (30 money sentences) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Underdog Woof, stock | 40.6 MB | non-commercial, no training on it | 1.2-3.3 s (not streaming) | 1.2-4.7x real time | - |
| **Underdog Woof, our streaming wrapper** | 40.6 MB | same | **80-100 ms** (1-2 threads) | 2.3-3.1x | **26-28 of 30** by transcript; most "misses" are Whistle writing "3,400 and 80" for a correct reading |
| Kyutai Pocket TTS 100M | 219 MB | CC-BY 4.0 | 68-127 ms | 3.2x | 27 of 30 (one real error: 126 said as 226) |
| Kyutai Pocket TTS 18M | small | CC-BY 4.0 | 76-85 ms | 3.0x | **20 of 30** (312.40 said as 31.40, 126 as 26, 17,903 as 1,793) |

- Streaming Woof is exact: its decoder is causal, so chunked decoding gives the same samples as whole-sentence decoding (difference about 1e-7). Schedule 1,2,4,8 frames had no playback underruns.
- Important: numpy's default thread count made Woof 8x slower here (800 ms to first sound). Pin to 1-2 threads.

Everything here was run on the dev laptop (i5-12450HX, 16 GB RAM, RTX 3050 6 GB, Windows 11) unless noted.

Scripts and raw results live in the session scratchpad (not in the repo):
`C:\Users\mgsuk\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\ccf816f539b7556e\84c9502f-eb89-46cc-b4c6-818cd19ea24b\scratchpad` (`spike\`, `expA\` to `expD\`). Copy them somewhere durable before a reboot if you want to keep them.

Status key: DONE = measured, PARTIAL = measured with known gaps, TODO = not yet run.

## 1. What exists (literature and products)

| System | Kind | What it shows | Why it is not our answer as is |
|---|---|---|---|
| OpenAI GPT-Live (`gpt-live-1`) | Closed speech-to-speech + delegation | About 0.8 s turn-taking latency (read off OpenAI's chart), delegates real work to a backend model | Paid per minute, cloud only, rephrases results, waits for end of turn before delegating |
| NVIDIA NemotronLabs VoiceChat (11B, Sept 2026) | Open full-duplex with tool calls | Best open full-duplex model; 448 ms smooth-turn latency | H100-class GPU, English, tool arguments right only 42%, no barge-in during tools, 2 min audio context |
| Moshi, PersonaPlex (7B) | Open full-duplex | 170-265 ms latency, good interruptions | Weak task quality (VoiceBench about 30), no tools |
| DuplexCascade (Interspeech 2026) | Cascade made full-duplex | Fine-tuning only a text LLM with control tokens (wait / respond / interrupted / backchannel) on 0.6 s micro-turns beats Moshi and PersonaPlex at turn-taking | Needs a 7B LLM in the loop every 0.6 s |
| Voice-Light (arXiv 2609.20995) | Cascade with speculative generation | Private speculative replies promoted after transcript checks: 667 ms vs 1,513 ms median | Two A10 GPUs, English, does not address tool side effects, learned turn head failed (12.5% recall) |
| LTS-VoiceAgent (EMNLP 2026) | "Think while listening" | Semantic trigger starts reasoning on prefixes | No tools, no numbers available to us |
| Talker-Reasoner, ConvFill, Ping-Ponder | Fast talker + slow reasoner | Filler speech hides reasoner latency | Talker is still an LLM |
| Full-Duplex-Bench v1/1.5/3 | Benchmarks | Pause handling, backchannels, interruptions, tool use under disfluency; self-correction is the most common failure everywhere | Use as our evaluation later |

### Speech to text: Cactus Whistle (16.9 MB, Apache-2.0) — DONE
- 3-5 s English sentences transcribed in 84-158 ms on CPU, 0 errors on plain questions.
- Streaming mode gives committed words plus a pending tail every 0.5 s chunk (pass 30-900 ms).
- German: 3 of 4 sentences perfect, one word wrong ("in bar" heard as "in Bahn").
- Weak spots: "net worth" heard as "network" (fixable with the `keywords` bias list), inconsistent number formatting ("3,400 and 80").
- `embed()` is not free: 94-162 ms per second of audio when measured while other jobs ran, and it slows a lot above 64 frames. Needs a clean re-measure.
- Alternative: Underdog Bark 3.0 (163 MB, English, 4.94% WER, non-commercial licence). Not tested.

### Text to speech — DONE
| Model | Size | Licence | First sound (CPU) | Speed | Numbers spoken right (30 money sentences) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Underdog Woof, stock | 40.6 MB | non-commercial, no training on it | 1.2-3.3 s (not streaming) | 1.2-4.7x real time | - |
| **Underdog Woof, our streaming wrapper** | 40.6 MB | same | **80-100 ms** (1-2 threads) | 2.3-3.1x | **26-28 of 30** by transcript; most "misses" are Whistle writing "3,400 and 80" for a correct reading |
| Kyutai Pocket TTS 100M | 219 MB | CC-BY 4.0 | 68-127 ms | 3.2x | 27 of 30 (one real error: 126 said as 226) |
| Kyutai Pocket TTS 18M | small | CC-BY 4.0 | 76-85 ms | 3.0x | **20 of 30** (312.40 said as 31.40, 126 as 26, 17,903 as 1,793) |

ChatGPT-plan models through Moneo's own sign-in, time to first word for a one-sentence reply:
`gpt-6-luna` 1.45-2.3 s, `gpt-6.1-sol` 2.3-2.7 s, `gpt-reserve` 1.6-2.1 s, `gpt-5.6-luna` 1.5-2.3 s.

700 spoken-style call utterances generated with GPT through the plan proxy (500 train, 200 test from separate personas), 7 routes: delegate-read, delegate-write, correction, meta, small talk, backchannel, incomplete.

| TF-IDF + linear SVM | 4.6 MB | 84.5% | 0 | 0 | 0.5 ms |

| Needle 3 zero-shot tool call | 35 MB | 21% | 27% | 67% | 1.2 s |
| LFM2.5-350M prompted | 379 MB | 32% | 0 | 100% | 8.6 s |
| Gemma 3 270M prompted | 292 MB | 11.5% | 0 | 0 | 0.6 s |
| SmolLM2-360M prompted | 386 MB | 23% | 0 | 73% | 0.4 s |

I'm comparing the Whistle-embedding heads against Smart Turn: the best GRU head reaches 91.9% on the English test subset, a linear probe with only 1.5K parameters reaches 91.5%, and Smart Turn's own figure on the same clips is still pending while its job runs. Meanwhile I'll start building the end-to-end speculative harness.

Next I'm sketching the end-to-end speculative harness, the headline experiment, though the CPU is tied up with two jobs, so I'll write it now and run it once the machine is clear. The plan is 30 test utterances across read, write, and small-talk routes, synthesized as 16 kHz audio with trailing silence and played back in real time in 80 ms frames. Each tick runs a VAD check, a partial-transcript router, and a speculation trigger that starts an acknowledgment phrase once a delegate route holds at 0.7 confidence for two ticks.

I'm setting up the commit logic: once silence passes 160 ms, I'll run the Smart Turn v3.2 check and commit right away if completion clears 0.5, otherwise wait up to 1.2 s. The ack audio goes out as soon as the turn is confirmed, and the reasoner's answer streams in after that, with the baseline cascade waiting a full 600 ms of silence for comparison.

I'm pinning down how the baseline and the comparison metrics will be measured: time to first audible sound, time to the real answer, wasted speculative reasoner calls, and wrong promotions. I'm also estimating roughly 70 reasoner calls in total, using a simple one-sentence finance prompt with no tools, since time to first token is the number that matters here.

To keep the baseline fair, I'll take the reasoner's time-to-first-token from the single speculative call and reuse it for the classic cascade, which removes network noise from the comparison. """End-to-end reflex loop on recorded speech, paced in real time.

Speculative reflex cascade (ours) vs a classic endpoint-then-go cascade built from the same parts:
  Whistle STT (re-run on the growing buffer), TF-IDF router, Smart Turn v3.2 end-of-turn check, streaming Woof TTS,
  gpt-6-luna on the ChatGPT plan as the thinking model (real network calls).
Ours: prepares the acknowledgement audio while the user is still talking, starts the thinking model at the first
160 ms of silence, and commits as soon as the turn detector says "done". Classic: waits 600 ms of silence first.

def main():
    mode = sys.argv[1]
    models = MODELS if mode == "test" else MODELS[:1]
    sessions = {m: build_session(os.path.join(MODELS_DIR, m)) for m in models}
    for m, s in sessions.items():
        print(m, [(i.name, i.shape) for i in s.get_inputs()], [(o.name, o.shape) for o in s.get_outputs()])
    if mode == "test":
        files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(HERE, "hf", "smart-turn-data-v3.2-test", "data", "*.parquet")))
        keep = None
    else:
        files = sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(HERE, "hf", "smart-turn-data-v3.2-train", "data", "*.parquet")))
        keep = set(np.load(os.path.join(HERE, "head_probs.npz"))["ids_val"].tolist())
    ids, ys = [], []
    probs = {m: [] for m in models}
    onnx_ms = {m: [] for m in models}
    feat_ms = []
    for path in files:
        pf = pq.ParquetFile(path)
        for rg in range(pf.metadata.num_row_groups):
            for r in pf.read_row_group(rg, columns=["audio", "id", "language", "endpoint_bool"]).to_pylist():
                if r["language"] != "eng" or (keep is not None and r["id"] not in keep):
                    continue
                x, sr = sf.read(io.BytesIO(r["audio"]["bytes"]), dtype="float32")
                if x.ndim > 1:
                    x = x.mean(1)
                t = time.perf_counter()
                feats = features(x)
                feat_ms.append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
                for m, s in sessions.items():
                    t = time.perf_counter()
                    out = s.run(None, {"input_features": feats})
                    onnx_ms[m].append((time.perf_counter() - t) * 1000)
                    probs[m].append(float(np.asarray(out[0]).reshape(-1)[0]))
                ids.append(r["id"])
                ys.append(int(r["endpoint_bool"]))
        print(os.path.basename(path), len(ids), "feat ms", round(float(np.median(feat_ms)), 2),
              {m: round(float(np.median(v)), 2) for m, v in onnx_ms.items()}, flush=True)
    np.savez(os.path.join(HERE, f"smartturn_probs_{mode}.npz"), ids=np.asarray(ids), y=np.asarray(ys, dtype=np.int8),
             feat_ms=np.asarray(feat_ms, dtype=np.float32),
             **{"p_" + m: np.asarray(v, dtype=np.float32) for m, v in probs.items()},
             **{"ms_" + m: np.asarray(v, dtype=np.float32) for m, v in onnx_ms.items()})
    y = np.asarray(ys)
    for m in models:
        p = np.asarray(probs[m]) > 0.5
        print(m, "n", len(y), "acc", (p == y).mean(), "FP/total", (p & (y == 0)).mean(), "FN/total", (~p & (y == 1)).mean())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
