tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendMessage
tools.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a listing from the system with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: WebFetch
tools.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

tools.name: WebSearch
tools.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_preview
tools.description: Check an HTML page before html_render. Returns PNG, contentHeight, and console output. Self-contained: inline <style> and <script>. Local images as absolute paths are inlined. Remote URLs load as-is. Theme and layout rules are in html_render.

path.description: Absolute .html file path.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__html_render
tools.description: Show a finished HTML page (chart, diagram, mockup) inline in this thread, above your final reply. Do not announce or restate the page. Frame fits height to 20000px. On mobile, content past the given height scrolls. Frame width is reply width (728px desktop, about 360px phones), on the thread background. Leave html, body, and the outer element with no background color, no outer card, border, banner title, or side padding. This wins over any rule that sets a page background. T3 adds an overridable 8px html gutter for selection rings and shadows. Use fluid widths within it. A box that needs its own background gets 16px padding and var(--radius) corners. Give charts fixed pixel heights. Let content set the height. Do not use vh units or height:100% on html or body. Both are rejected or loop. Use theme CSS variables on :root, not fixed colors: --background, --foreground, --muted, --card, --popover, --secondary, --border, --ring, --primary, --accent, --destructive, --warning, --success, --info, --code-background (most have a matching -foreground; accent, destructive, and warning also have -surface), --chart-1 to --chart-6, --radius, --font-sans, --font-mono. The base sheet sets background, text, and font.

tools.name: mcp__t3-code__request_secret

content.content:
The arXiv abstract page gives only a high-level overview of SoulX-Duplug. It doesn't cover several things you asked about.

**What the page says:**
- **Purpose:** A "plug-and-play streaming state prediction module" for full-duplex spoken dialogue systems.
- **Method:** It jointly performs streaming ASR and uses textual information to identify user intent, "effectively serving as a semantic VAD."
- **Results:** The authors say it enables low-latency streaming dialogue state control and that a system built on it outperforms existing full-duplex models in turn management and latency. The page gives no numbers.
- **Evaluation:** The authors introduce SoulX-Duplug-Eval, which extends widely used benchmarks with better bilingual coverage.
- **Code/weights:** The authors state they have open-sourced SoulX-Duplug and SoulX-Duplug-Eval. The page does not name a software license. The "view license" link is the arXiv paper license, not the code license.
- **Status:** v1, submitted 16 March 2026 to Interspeech 2026, under review.

**Not covered on this page:**
- Its specific states, and the audio and text input/output format
- Model size
- Latency figures
- How it integrates into a cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS pipeline
- Quantitative comparison against VAD or Smart Turn
- The software license of the released code and weights

The HTML and PDF versions linked from the page (arxiv.org/html/2603.14877v1 and /pdf/2603.14877) probably contain these details, and the GitHub or Hugging Face release would show the license.

content.content:
**Architecture:** The paper proposes a frontend-backend design. A duplex speech-to-text frontend handles the conversation, and a text-based backend LLM handles tool calls. The frontend learns to emit a delegation token when a task needs a tool.

**Frontend-backend communication:** The frontend forwards streaming ASR transcripts to the backend LLM. The backend returns tool-call results to the frontend.

**Tool result injection:** Results are injected back into the frontend through a lightweight prefill-and-repeat mechanism. The frontend then speaks the answer using streaming TTS.

**Latency:** The abstract says the design largely preserves regular duplex turn-taking, interruption handling, and low-latency interaction, because it requires minimal changes to the frontend model. It gives no specific latency figures.

**Accuracy and results:**
- Single-turn tool-call evaluation: 92-97% tool-call recall, competitive tool-call prediction, and 81.2% accuracy in rejecting irrelevant calls.
- With a larger backend (e.g., Qwen3-235B-A22B), results are competitive on Full-Duplex-Bench-V3 with open and closed models.
- On EVA-Bench, it significantly outperforms GPT-realtime-mini and Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct.

**Limitations:** The page does not state limitations explicitly. The evaluation shown is single-turn tool calling, and the strongest results depend on a large backend model. Those are the only constraints I can identify from the page, and the full paper would be needed to confirm others.

**Problem:** In LLM-based full-duplex voice services, the server can generate output and advance dialogue state faster than the client plays it. A user's next utterance may then refer to content they never heard. The authors call this "Generative Context Mis-anchoring (GCM)."

**Approach:** PACE is a provider-independent middleware layer that ties the model-facing context to the client's playback boundary, which serves as a proxy for what the user could have heard. The abstract describes this boundary as "a system-observable proxy" for what the user could have heard.

**Interruption handling:** After an interruption, PACE repairs the context so it excludes assistant content that never reached playback. The abstract says this is done while keeping generation low-latency across different voice runtimes.

**Mechanism details:** The abstract is light on specifics. It states that the authors implemented PACE's audio-only projection path end to end in a browser-based realtime voice assistant. It uses a black-box speech model without modifying the model service. How playback position is measured and how context is rewritten are not described in the abstract, so the full paper would be needed for those.

**Results:**
- **GCM-Bench** (a new dataset of 108 playback-relative referent-anchoring cases): Referent Anchoring Accuracy rose from 25.0% to 96.3% over a cancellation-only baseline.
- **Full-Duplex-Bench v1** (200 interruption samples): PACE preserved interruption response quality.

The authors conclude that grounding model context in actual playback is a practical way to keep full-duplex dialogue consistent.

content.text:
The full end-to-end timing run (26 simulated calls, real ChatGPT-plan thinking model) is running on an otherwise idle CPU; I'll pick up automatically when it finishes.

**Results so far**

| Part | Finding |
|---|---|
| Speech to text (Whistle) | 74–158 ms per sentence on CPU. |
| Voice | I made Woof stream: first sound in about 80–100 ms, and the audio is identical to the original. It reads 26–28 of 30 money sentences back correctly. The small Pocket TTS model only manages 20 of 30. |
| Thinking model | ChatGPT-plan models take 1.5–2.7 s to their first word, so they can't sit in the instant path. |
| Router | TF-IDF + logistic regression (4.6 MB, 0.5 ms) dropped 0 of 88 money questions. Tiny generative models scored 11–32% and took 0.4–8.6 s. Caveat: cross-validation gives only about 72% overall, so it needs more training data. |
| Turn detector | A 105K-weight head on Whistle's own features reaches 91.9% on the Smart Turn test clips. The head-to-head against Smart Turn itself hasn't run yet. |
| Barge-in | A naive pipeline interrupts itself on every echo (24 of 24). Echo cancelling plus my "ignore words the assistant is saying" filter cuts false stops to about 8%. It is still too slow (about 1 s to stop) and missed 6 of 24 interruptions in a harsh synthetic test. |
| First end-to-end test (one call) | Our first sound came 358 ms after the user stopped, against 2,550 ms for a classic pipeline. |

The parallel subagents hit your usage limit twice within minutes, so I finished their experiments myself from the files they left.

Still to do after this run:
- Smart Turn comparison on the same clips
- Fix the barge-in speed
- Pre-generated and early-prepared acknowledgement audio
- The options with architecture diagrams

The log is at [LOG.md](C:\Users\mgsuk\.t3\worktrees\Moneo\t3-846dd64c-f0b28664becb1320\research\voice-duplex\LOG.md) (uncommitted); it doesn't yet include the latest barge-in rerun or turn-detector numbers.

"""Talker test: tiny local chat models answer 30 small-talk utterances; gpt-6-luna writes the reference and judges blind.
Usage: talker.py local <key> <gguf> [threads]   |   talker.py luna   |   talker.py judge"""
import random, re, sys, time
import numpy as np
from common import *
from evallib import save_result

test = read_jsonl(os.path.join(DATA, "test.jsonl"))
small = [r for r in test if r["label"] == "SMALLTALK"][:30]
OUT = os.path.join(B, "talker"); os.makedirs(OUT, exist_ok=True)
SYS = ("You are Moneo, a relaxed friend on a voice call. Reply to what the user just said in ONE short, warm, casual spoken sentence "
       "(under 15 words). Never state any money fact, amount, price or balance. Never say you did, will do or are doing anything. "
       "No emojis, no lists, no questions about money.")


def user_msg(r):
    return r["text"]


mode = sys.argv[1]
if mode == "local":
    key, path = sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]
    threads = int(sys.argv[4]) if len(sys.argv) > 4 else 4
    from llama_cpp import Llama
    llm = Llama(model_path=path, n_ctx=1024, n_threads=threads, verbose=False)
    llm.create_chat_completion(messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYS}, {"role": "user", "content": "hi"}], max_tokens=4)  # warm up + cache the system prompt
    rows = []
    for r in small:
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); first = None; n = 0; text = ""
        for ch in llm.create_chat_completion(messages=[{"role": "system", "content": SYS}, {"role": "user", "content": user_msg(r)}],
                                             max_tokens=40, temperature=0.3, top_p=0.9, seed=1, stream=True):
            d = ch["choices"][0]["delta"].get("content")
            if d:
                if first is None: first = time.perf_counter()
                n += 1; text += d
        end = time.perf_counter()
        rows.append({"id": r["id"], "user": r["text"], "reply": text.strip(), "first_ms": round(((first or end) - t0) * 1000, 1),
                     "total_ms": round((end - t0) * 1000, 1), "tokens": n, "tok_s": round((n - 1) / (end - first), 1) if first and n > 1 and end > first else None})
        print(rows[-1], flush=True)
    write_jsonl(os.path.join(OUT, f"{key}_t{threads}.jsonl"), rows)

content.text:
The full timing run is in: measured from the end of the user's speech, our pipeline's first sound comes after a median 509 ms on money requests, against 2,509 ms for a classic pipeline. The answer itself arrives only about 270 ms sooner, and small talk is no faster. Timings are relative to the test's speech-end marker, so the gaps are more reliable than the absolute numbers.

**End-to-end results (26 simulated calls, real ChatGPT-plan thinking model, idle CPU)**

| Measure (ms, median) | Ours | Classic pipeline | Classic with a filler phrase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Money requests: first sound | 509 | 2,509 | 778 |
| Money requests: answer starts | 2,238 | 2,509 | 2,509 |
| Small talk: first sound | 2,638 | 2,498 | 2,498 |

- **First reaction:** 509 ms compares with GPT-Live's roughly 0.8 s claim, but the slowest tenth of our calls took 1.7 s or more.
- **Answer speed:** the thinking model's 1.7 s to a first sentence dominates. Starting it at the first pause saves little; bigger gains need read-only data fetched while the user is still talking, which this run did not test.
- **Small talk:** it goes to the cloud model, and the turn detector often waited for the 1.2 s fallback. It needs a local talker or phrase bank.
- **Mid-sentence pauses:** all 4 paused test sentences made us answer too early (5 early answers in total, against 4 for the classic pipeline). In 2 of the 4 the final transcript also lost half the sentence.
- **Whistle slowdown:** transcription jumps from about 110 ms to about 900 ms once the audio buffer passes roughly 5 s, so it needs a sliding window or its streaming mode.
- **Acknowledgement audio:** it was ready before the user finished in 11 of 17 money requests.
- **Failures:** one thinking-model call hung for 38 s, so timeouts and retries are needed. 6 early thinking-model calls were thrown away.

The Smart Turn comparison is running now. After it I'll test the tiny local talkers (LFM2.5-350M, Gemma 270M), update the log, and send the options with architecture diagrams.

input.old_string:
### Turn detector — PARTIAL
- Baseline: Pipecat Smart Turn v3.2 (8 MB ONNX, BSD-2).
- Our idea: a tiny head on Whistle's own encoder frames. Embeddings for about 6,300 train and 7,900 test English clips of the Smart Turn v3.2 data are computed; training and the head-to-head are running (results to be added).
input.new_string:
### Turn detector — DONE (first pass)
Same 1,583 English test clips of the Smart Turn v3.2 data (heads trained on about 6,300 English train clips, Whistle encoder frozen):

| Detector | Trained weights | Accuracy | Cuts the user off | Misses the end | CPU time |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smart Turn v3.2 (8 MB ONNX, BSD-2) | 8M | **95.0%** | 6.4% | 3.6% | 20 ms + 6 ms features |
| Whistle frames, linear on mean + last + last-5 | 1,537 | 92.7% | 9.3% | 5.1% | under 1 ms on top of Whistle |
| Whistle frames, small GRU | 105K | 91.9% | 10.2% | 6.0% | under 1 ms on top of Whistle |

- Smart Turn wins by about 2 points, with a home advantage (it was trained on the full train split of this data). Use it for now.
- A 1.5K-weight probe at 92.7% shows Whistle's features already carry most of the turn signal. More data, an unfrozen top layer and finance-call audio are the way to close the gap; that is a laptop-sized fine-tune.
- Training of larger heads was stopped early to free the CPU; `expA\train_results.json` has the five finished heads.
- Not tested: telling a backchannel from the start of an interruption from audio alone.

### Small-talk talker — DONE (zero-shot)
30 small-talk lines, blind-judged by gpt-6-luna (1-5):

| Model | Size | Whole reply (CPU) | Naturalness | Fits what was said | Unsafe flags |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gpt-6-luna (cloud) | - | 2,026 ms | 4.83 | 4.73 | 2 |
| Gemma 3 270M Q8 | 292 MB | **94 ms** | 3.23 | 2.77 | 1 |
| LFM2.5-350M Q4 | 229 MB | 176 ms | 3.03 | 2.53 | 3 |
| SmolLM2-360M Q8 | 386 MB | 236 ms | 2.77 | 2.17 | 5 |

- The tiny models are 10-20x faster than the cloud model but often parrot the user or say something odd ("luckycardwin", emojis). Not usable as is.
- This is the best fine-tuning target found: distil a few thousand gpt-6-luna small-talk replies into Gemma 270M or LFM2.5-350M with LoRA on the 6 GB GPU. Not run yet.

### End-to-end timing — DONE (simulated calls)
26 recorded utterances (10 money questions, 6 money statements, 6 small talk, 4 with a 0.7 s pause in the middle), played in real time into the full loop: Whistle, TF-IDF router, Smart Turn v3.2, streaming Woof, and gpt-6-luna on the ChatGPT plan as a stand-in thinking model without tools. "Classic" is the same parts with a 600 ms silence endpoint. Times are from the end of the user's speech; the speech-end marker sits a little late, so compare columns rather than reading absolutes.

| Median ms (90th percentile) | Ours | Classic | Classic + filler phrase |
|---|---|---|---|
| Money requests, first sound (17) | **509** (1,719) | 2,509 (3,048) | 778 (1,449) |
| Money requests, answer starts | 2,238 (3,322) | 2,509 (3,048) | 2,509 |
| Small talk, first sound (8) | 2,638 (4,046) | 2,498 (3,672) | 2,498 |

- First reaction beats GPT-Live's roughly 0.8 s claim at the median, not at the tail.
- Starting the thinking model at the first 160 ms pause only buys about 270 ms on the answer: the model's 1.7 s to a first sentence dominates. Bigger wins need read-only data fetched while the user is still talking (not measured: this run had no tools).
- The acknowledgement audio was ready before the user finished in 11 of 17 money requests.
- Small talk is no faster: it went to the cloud model and the turn check often fell back to the 1.2 s timer.
- Mid-sentence pauses: all 4 paused sentences triggered an early answer (5 early answers in total vs 4 for classic); in 2 of the 4 the final transcript lost half the sentence. Open problem.
- Whistle slows from about 110 ms to about 900 ms once the buffer passes roughly 5 s. Use its streaming mode or a sliding window.
- 6 early thinking-model calls were discarded; 1 call hung for 38 s (needs a timeout and retry).

content.text:
Nothing open beats GPT-Live out of the box on this laptop, and what I built does not beat it yet either. It reacts faster at the median on money requests and costs nothing per minute, but true full-duplex behaviour (barge-in, mid-sentence pauses) is still unsolved. I recommend option A below as the thing to keep building.

## Options

| | Option | For | Against |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | **Speculative reflex cascade** (diagram above): tiny local models react instantly, the Moneo chat agent starts early in the background | Median first sound 509 ms on money requests; runs on CPU; every part swappable; exact numbers; free per minute; several small fine-tunes possible | Barge-in and pause handling not there yet; small talk is slow until the talker is fine-tuned |
| B | Classic pipeline with a filler phrase (speech to text, wait for silence, model, voice) | Simplest; about a week of work | 778 ms first sound; turn-based, so not what you asked for |
| C | DuplexCascade style: a small LLM emits control tokens every 0.6 s | Best published turn-taking for a cascade | Needs a local 4–7B model on a GPU, which you ruled out; cloud models are too slow for it |
| D | Open speech-to-speech model (NVIDIA VoiceChat 11B, PersonaPlex) | Real full-duplex in one model | Needs a datacentre GPU, English only, tool arguments right 42% of the time |
| E | Keep GPT-Live as a paid choice next to A in the same call screen | Safe fallback while A matures | Two voice paths to maintain |

## What the tests showed

- **Answer speed:** starting the thinking model at the first pause only saves about 270 ms, because ChatGPT-plan models need 1.5–2.7 s to their first word. The larger win should be fetching read-only data while you are still talking; I did not measure that.
- **Voice:** I made Woof stream. First sound comes in 80–100 ms and the audio is identical to the original. It read 26–28 of 30 money sentences back correctly; the small Pocket TTS model managed 20.
- **Woof licence:** it is non-commercial and forbids training on its audio. Pocket TTS 100M is the permissive fallback (27 of 30).
- **Router:** no generative model needed. TF-IDF plus logistic regression (4.6 MB, 0.5 ms) dropped 0 of 88 money questions, while tiny LLMs scored 11–32%. Cross-validation gives only about 72% overall, so it needs more training data.
- **Turn detector:** Smart Turn v3.2 scores 95.0%. My 1,537-weight head on Whistle's own features scores 92.7%, so Smart Turn stays for now.
- **Small talk:** tiny local chat models reply in 94–236 ms but rate about 3 of 5 for naturalness against 4.8 for the cloud model. Distilling the cloud model into one of them is the clearest fine-tune.
- **Barge-in:** a naive pipeline interrupts itself on every echo (24 of 24). Echo cancelling plus my self-speech filter cuts false stops to about 8%. It still missed 6 of 24 interruptions and took about 1 s to stop, in a harsh synthetic test.
- **Mid-sentence pauses:** all 4 paused test sentences triggered an early answer.
- **Whistle:** transcription slows from about 110 ms to about 900 ms once the audio passes roughly 5 s, so it needs a sliding window.

## Not done

- No side-by-side run against GPT-Live; its 0.8 s is OpenAI's own figure.
- No real microphone and speaker test; all audio was synthetic.
- No fine-tuning yet, and the pre-generated phrase bank is untested.
- The parallel Fable subagents hit your usage limit twice within minutes, so I finished their experiments myself.
- I stopped the local proxy that used your ChatGPT sign-in. It made roughly 300 calls on your plan.

## Next steps I'd take

1. Fix barge-in with a faster "user is speaking over me" detector, tested on a real mic.
2. Measure read-only prefetch against the real Moneo chat agent with tools.

content.text:
**Short version:** our own voice call is possible and already reacts faster than GPT-Live on money questions, but it is not better overall yet.

**What works**
- **First reaction:** about 0.5 s after you stop talking (GPT-Live says about 0.8 s).
- **All tiny and local:** speech-to-text (Whistle), voice (Woof, which I made stream), turn detection and routing run on the laptop CPU, free per minute.
- **Numbers:** Woof reads money amounts correctly almost every time.
- **Router:** a 4.6 MB classic classifier beats every tiny LLM I tried, in half a millisecond.

**What doesn't work yet**
- **Interrupting Moneo while it talks:** too slow (about 1 s) and it missed 6 of 24 interruptions.
- **Pausing mid-sentence:** it answers too early.
- **Small talk:** tiny local chat models are fast but say odd things; one needs fine-tuning.
- **Actual answers:** only about 0.3 s faster, because the ChatGPT model itself takes 1.5–2.7 s to start.

**The design I recommend**
1. Small local models listen and react instantly ("let me check your groceries").
2. The Moneo chat agent starts working before you finish the sentence.
3. Amounts are spoken exactly as Moneo wrote them, and writes stay tap-only cards.
4. Every part can be swapped (Woof or another voice, ChatGPT or Claude or an API key).

**Next**
1. Fix interruptions, tested with a real microphone.
2. Fetch your data while you're still talking, to speed up real answers.
3. Fine-tune a tiny model for small talk.

**Caveats:** everything was tested with synthetic voices, not a real mic, and I never ran GPT-Live side by side. Woof's licence is non-commercial.

Details are in `research\voice-duplex\LOG.md` (uncommitted).

content.text:
**The options** were five ways to build the voice call:
- **A:** our own thing — tiny local models react instantly and the Moneo chat agent starts early in the background.
- **B:** a plain pipeline (listen, wait for silence, think, speak) with a filler phrase.
- **C:** a small LLM that decides every 0.6 s whether to wait, speak or stop. It needs a GPU model you ruled out.
- **D:** one big open speech-to-speech model. It needs a datacentre GPU.
- **E:** keep GPT-Live as a paid choice next to A.

**The Whistle embedding work** was about knowing when you've finished talking, not interruptions. Whistle already computes audio features to transcribe, so I trained a tiny classifier (about 1,500 weights) on those features to say "done" or "still talking". It got 92.7% against 95.0% for Smart Turn, the existing detector. Interruptions were a separate test (echo canceller plus ignoring words Moneo is saying itself). Using the Whistle features to tell "mm-hm" from a real interruption was planned but never run.

**The subagents:** all four were cut off by your usage limit, three of them twice. None is running now. Their scripts and partial results stayed on disk, and I finished every experiment myself from those files. Everything is copied into `research\voice-duplex\experiments`.

**What I suggest:** keep design A, and make the duplex part one small trained model instead of the separate pieces and rules I used.

1. **Real audio first.** Build a small browser test call with a real mic and speaker, and record real calls. Everything so far used synthetic voices, which is why interruptions looked bad and can't be trusted either way.
2. **One "duplex controller" model.** A tiny model on Whistle's features that says every 80 ms: you're talking, you're done, you're thinking, that was just "mm-hm", or you're interrupting. It also hears what Moneo is playing, so it learns to ignore Moneo's own voice. This replaces the voice detector, Smart Turn and my rules, and it is the part worth publishing.
3. **Early data fetching.** While you're still talking, fetch read-only data for the real Moneo agent and cache it, so answers come sooner. Writes stay tap-only cards.
4. **Fine-tune the small parts:**
   - a tiny chat model for small talk, taught by the big model;
   - Whistle on money words and number formats;
   - more training data for the router;
   - Pocket TTS on amounts, as the open voice — Woof's licence forbids training.
5. **Score it properly.** Run the public full-duplex benchmarks plus our own Moneo call test, side by side with GPT-Live.

I'd start with step 1, because steps 2 and 5 depend on real recordings.

The search didn't turn up a paper that uses the exact "text-informed" or "transcript-aware" framing. It did surface several related approaches.

- **Patent prior art on monitoring TTS output:** A patent (US 7,062,440) is described as monitoring text-to-speech output to effect control of barge-in. In that scheme, barge-in is only acted on during system output when speech is recognized on the input channel (the barge-in control is arranged to permit barge-in at any time but only takes notice of barge-in during output by the speech system on the basis of a speech input being recognized in the input channel).
- **Echo-aware detection using the TTS reference:** A Coval blog post recommends using the known output as a reference: use the known TTS output as a reference signal. If significant speech energy remains after echo cancellation, classify it as a genuine user interruption (barge-in). This is reference-signal AEC plus a residual-energy test, not transcript matching.
- **Practical text matching in a bug report:** A GitHub issue from a Jetson voice framework shows a text-match filter working as intended. Its logs include 8 tts_text_match suppressions: echo suppression is working and correctly rejecting the assistant's own voice. The same report says the barge-in filter rejected real interruptions. Only 1 of 30 barge-in attempts was confirmed during a 16-minute unscripted session, and the author concluded that if they overlap and no threshold separates them, the answer is a different detection signal, not a different number. This is a single user report, not peer-reviewed.
- **Vendor-side symptoms:** A Microsoft Q&A thread describes intermittent barge-in with echo cancellation enabled, where sometimes the microphone does not detect my input at all.

Overall, the sources support using the known TTS reference signal or text, but I found no clear published method that conditions barge-in decisions on the system prompt text specifically. Searching for academic terms such as "echo-aware" or "self-echo" ASR with TTS-conditioned ASR may find more.

The search surfaced several 2026 voice activity projection (VAP) papers on turn-taking, but nothing on speculative LLM responses started before the end of a turn, which was the core of your query.

- **Sensor-augmented VAP (SIGDIAL 2026):** The authors add head-motion signals from earable sensors to acoustic VAP. They conclude that head-motion cues are effective for enhancing turn-taking prediction. The qualitative analysis adds that IMU signals contribute to more stable prediction of future voice activity, particularly in single-speaker intervals and around turn-shift boundaries.
- **Child–adult VAP (IWSDS 2026):** The authors compared a silence-threshold model with VAP. VAP, using acoustic cues occurring before the silence, achieved much higher accuracy. They also note that silence is an unreliable cue, as it can equally signal a within-turn pause or a turn completion.
- **MuVAP (arXiv, June 2026):** This is a multimodal, multiparty extension of VAP. It extends Voice Activity Projection by grounding acoustic predictions in face tracks, enabling speaker-aware turn-taking predictions from a monaural audio stream and a single camera view. It outperforms strong baselines on Shift-Hold and next-speaker prediction tasks across two- and three-speaker settings.
- **Related items:** A reference list cites a 2026 arXiv paper, DualTurn (arXiv:2603.08216), on learning turn-taking from dual-channel generative speech pretraining, and a 2026 paper called TurnNat on automatically evaluating turn-taking naturalness. I only saw their titles and citations, not their contents.

The search did not find work on speculative or early LLM response generation before end-of-turn detection. A follow-up search on that specific topic, such as "speculative response before end of turn spoken dialogue," would be needed to cover it.

The search didn't turn up anything that matches your exact idea of a runtime check that verifies TTS audio before it plays. The results cover offline TTS evaluation, mostly by round-tripping audio through ASR.

- **Round-trip entity testing:** AssemblyAI's guide defines a round-trip entity accuracy metric, which measures how many entities survive text → TTS → STT. It recommends reporting pass rates per entity type rather than one blended score. It describes the share of entities that survive a trip from text to TTS audio and back to text through a strong speech-to-text model. It says to synthesize each test sentence, transcribe the audio, normalize both sides, and check whether the expected entity appears.
- **Why WER isn't enough:** The same guide argues that word error rate alone misses what matters on calls. Hamming's guide makes a similar point, noting that TTS checks should cover names, numbers, and dates.

content.text:
No, the last plan was not new enough. Its main piece, a tiny trained head on speech-recognition features, is already in Voice-Light (Sept 2026), and it worked badly there. Here is what I think is new and thesis-sized.

## The core idea

Moneo has two advantages a general voice model lacks:
- It knows exactly what it is saying at every moment.
- It knows roughly what you are going to say, because money questions are a narrow, predictable set.

Build every small model around those two facts. Working title: **"Know what you said, guess what they'll say: full-duplex voice from under 100 MB on a CPU."**

## Four contributions

1. **Self-aware listening.** One tiny model hears the mic *and* what Moneo is playing (its audio and its text). Every 80 ms it says: you're talking, you're done, you're thinking, that was "mm-hm", or you're interrupting.
   - It replaces the voice detector, turn detector, my text filter and the rules.
   - Training data is nearly free: the laptop plays its own voice through its speaker and records it, so real echo comes with perfect labels.
   - What exists today is echo cancelling plus simple text matching. A hobby project reports that confirming only 1 real interruption in 30, the same failure I measured.

2. **Predictive early work.** A small model predicts how your sentence will end and when. Reads and the thinking model start on that guess, with every tool marked "read" or "write".
   - Reads may run early and are cached; writes never do.
   - Nothing is heard or saved until the real sentence confirms the guess.
   - Voice-Light starts replies early but only at a pause, and says nothing about tools.

3. **Checked speech.** Before a sentence with numbers plays, Whistle re-listens to it (about 100 ms) and confirms every amount, and a wrong take is re-made. I found this only as an offline test method, never as a live guard.

4. **A benchmark.** Recorded money calls with pauses, corrections, "mm-hm"s and interruptions, run against GPT-Live and the public full-duplex benchmarks. Without this, nobody will believe the rest.

## What gets trained (all fit the 6 GB GPU)

- The self-aware listening model (new, small).
- The sentence-ending predictor.
- Whistle on money words and number formats.
- A tiny small-talk model taught by the big one.
- Pocket TTS on amounts (Woof's licence forbids training).

## Risks

- Voice-Light's learned head failed when trained on synthetic audio. Mine could too; real self-recorded echo and real call recordings are the defence.
- "New" rests on a handful of searches. A proper literature review comes first.
- Predicting sentence endings may only pay off in a narrow domain. That is fine for Moneo, but it limits the claim.

## Order

1. Literature review to confirm each novelty claim.
2. Real-mic test call in the browser, plus the self-recording data rig.
3. Self-aware listening model: the hardest and most valuable part.
4. Predictive early work against the real Moneo agent.
5. Checked speech.
6. Benchmark and write-up.

Sources:
- [Voice-Light](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.20995)
- [Helios barge-in issue](https://github.com/UbiquitousDynamics/helios-ai-jetson-framework/issues/12)
- [AssemblyAI on round-trip TTS testing](https://www.assemblyai.com/blog/how-to-evaluate-tts-voice-agents)
- [Voice activity projection, IWSDS 2026](https://aclanthology.org/2026.iwsds-1.34/)

The search turned up the original Textual Echo Cancellation paper and a few related works, but no direct follow-up paper that extends TEC itself.

- **Original paper:** Ding, Jia, Hu, and Wang (Google) introduced TEC on arXiv in 2020, with a later revision in 2021. The system uses a sequence-to-sequence model with multi-source attention that takes both the microphone mixture signal and the source text of the TTS playback as inputs, and predicts the enhanced audio. Its main advantage is that the text sequence is much smaller than the raw acoustic signal of the TTS playback and can be transmitted before the playback is synthesized.
- **Patent:** A Google patent titled "Textual echo cancelation" (US 11482244) describes the same approach, using the text that the TTS system already generates.
- **Barge-in context:** A separate patent on reference signal suppression (US 9240183) addresses barge-in directly. It suppresses TTS output from captured audio so the user's interrupting speech can still be recognized, and it names adaptive filtering as one way to do that.
- **Limitation noted by later work:** Cornell et al. (Amazon, arXiv 2111.10639) cite the TEC approach and point out that it is only applicable to TTS playback and does not generalize to other forms of playback audio such as podcasts or music. Their own method, implicit AEC, instead feeds the reference signal directly into the keyword-spotting or device-directed speech classifier.

I didn't find a follow-up paper that extends TEC specifically, so if you need one, a search on citing papers or on the arXiv listing for 2008.06006 would be the next step.

Its temporal-cache benchmark achieved a median of 30.6x speedup on cache hits. It also reports that pure semantic caching can fail on parameter-rich queries, which matters for tool calls.

The paper you're likely thinking of is **"Personalized Predictive ASR for Latency Reduction in Voice Assistants"** by Andreas Schwarz, Di He, Maarten Van Segbroeck, Mohammed Hethnawi, and Ariya Rastrow, accepted at Interspeech 2023 (arXiv:2305.13794).

- **Core idea:** Prefetching works by sending a preliminary ASR hypothesis downstream so a response can be prepared and cached. Prefetching involves passing a preliminary ASR hypothesis to downstream systems in order to prefetch and cache a response.
- **Hit case:** If the final hypothesis after endpointing matches the early one, the stored response is served immediately, which reduces latency (the cached response can be delivered to the user, thus saving latency).
- **Their extension:** The authors predict the full utterance from a partial one and prefetch against that predicted text. They also study the trade-off between latency savings when predictions succeed and extra cost when they fail. They introduce two personalization approaches and investigate the tradeoff between potential latency gains from successful predictions and the cost increase from failed predictions.
- **Evaluation:** The methods were tested on an internal voice assistant dataset and the public SLURP dataset (We evaluate our methods on an internal voice assistant dataset as well as the public SLURP dataset.).

A related follow-up is **"Speculative Speech Recognition" by Yusuf, Baskar, Rosenberg, and Ramabhadran** (arXiv:2407.04641). It has the ASR run ahead of the audio and uses a language model to predict likely completions for the partial ASR hypothesis. The authors cite the Schwarz et al. work as the prefetching precedent.

I ran one search, so I haven't checked the full PDF's latency numbers or the exact results tables.

**SoulX-Duplug: key details (from the page)**

- **States predicted:** Five state tokens: user_idle (silence or noise), user_nonidle (meaningful speech), user_backchannel, user_complete (assistant may take the turn), and user_incomplete (user paused mid-thought, so the assistant should wait).
- **Architecture:** A plug-in module that jointly does streaming ASR and state prediction, interleaving audio, text, and state tokens. Audio is encoded by a frozen GLM-4-Voice tokenizer, projected by an MLP adapter, and fed to an LLM. The page does not give a total parameter count. The LLM backbone is Qwen3-0.6B, with LoRA (rank 32) for state-prediction training.
- **Inputs:** User-side audio only, at 12.5 Hz tokens. Inference uses an external ASR (Paraformer for Mandarin, SenseVoice Small for English) to supply text via teacher forcing.
- **Chunk size and latency:** Chunks are 160 ms, with a 1160 ms receptive field (960 ms look-back, 40 ms look-ahead). The theoretical average latency is 240 ms. Measured latency is 205 ms (EN) and 295 ms (ZH), about 250 ms on average.
- **Echo/own-speech handling:** Not addressed.
- **Backchannels and interruptions during system speech:** A user_backchannel state exists. The system is evaluated on backchannel (Resume Rate) and interruption (Respond Rate, Stop Latency) tests. English stop latency is 0.45 s, and Chinese is 0.38 s. The page does not describe the mechanism for handling interruptions beyond these states.
- **Training data:**
  - ASR: about 47,000 h of Mandarin and 31,000 h of English.
  - State prediction: Fisher (English, about a thousand hours) and an in-house Mandarin corpus (about ten thousand hours).
  - Noise augmentation uses MUSAN and ESC-50. Labels were produced with Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct.
- **Results vs. other systems:**
  - Easy Turn testset, average accuracy: SoulX-Duplug 83.32% (EN) vs. Smart Turn V2 69.25% (EN), and 84.33% (ZH) vs. Easy Turn 97.00% (ZH). The page says SoulX is about 3% below the strongest non-streaming pipeline, which is SenseVoice + TEN Turn Detection at 86.10% (EN) and Paraformer + TEN at 87.99% (ZH).
  - Full-Duplex-Bench: SoulX-Duplug's Turn Taking TOR is 0.933 (EN) and 0.994 (ZH). The page reports it outperforms Freeze-Omni and Gemini Live on several metrics, and it compares favorably on overall turn management and latency.
  - Latency: FlexDuo's VAD-based approach is reported at 500 ms.
- **Hardware:** Training on NVIDIA H20 GPUs. Evaluation in simulated streaming on a single NVIDIA L20 GPU. CPU use is not mentioned.
- **Licence:** The page says the code and SoulX-Duplug-Eval are open-sourced on GitHub (Soul-AILab/SoulX-Duplug), but it does not state the software licence. The page itself is under an arXiv perpetual non-exclusive license.

**Problem:** In full-duplex spoken dialogue models, text generation, speech synthesis, and audio playback run asynchronously. The model's internal record of what it said can therefore differ from what the user actually heard. The paper calls recovering from an interruption while tracking the model's realized speech "anchor interruption."

**Method:** The proposed approach, Self-Listening, interleaves user speech, the model's text, and the model's played speech. The realized output is fed back to the model as an input stream, so interruption recovery is grounded in what the user heard. The paper also introduces AnchorSpeech, a dataset of structured, ordered responses with train and test splits that track which items were actually spoken. AnchorSpeech-test checks whether a model responds consistently with the last completed item before an interruption.

**Model size:** Not stated in the provided content.

**Results:** The abstract reports that models with the self-listening mechanism achieve better anchoring performance than full-duplex baselines. No specific metrics or numbers appear in the provided text.

**Limitations:** The provided content does not discuss limitations. It is also only the arXiv abstract page, so the full paper may contain more detail.

**Known text or audio of its own output:** The method uses the audio of the model's played speech, not the known text it intended to say. The model is fed the realized speech output, which reflects what was actually played. The page does not specify how that audio is encoded or processed.

**AgenticCache** is a planning framework for embodied AI agents that reuses cached plans to avoid calling an LLM at every step.

- **What is cached:** Frequent plan transitions. The authors observe "plan locality": the next plan is largely predictable from the current one.
- **How the cache is consulted:** Each agent queries this runtime cache instead of calling the LLM for each step.
- **Background validator:** A Cache Updater runs asynchronously, calling the LLM to validate and refine cached entries. The abstract doesn't describe how this works in detail.
- **Results:** Across four multi-agent embodied benchmarks and three models (12 configurations), the authors report an average 22% gain in task success rate, 65% lower simulation latency, and 50% lower token usage.
- **Lookup cache or trained model:** The abstract describes a runtime lookup cache of plan transitions. It doesn't mention training or distilling a small model. The full paper would be needed to confirm the mechanism.

I ran one search. It turned up a cluster of recent work on starting computation before a speaker finishes, but nothing that specifically covers database queries or enumerating candidate answers before end of utterance.

- **Predictive ASR and end-of-utterance (EOU) detection:** One arXiv paper (2409.19990) trains an encoder-decoder ASR model to predict upcoming words and forecast the endpoint up to about 300 ms early, which gives downstream NLP modules time to start working. It reports the model can predict upcoming words and estimate future EOU events up to 300ms prior to the actual EOU.
- **Speculative speech recognition:** A separate paper (2407.04641) frames the goal as producing the full transcript before the user finishes. Its baseline pairs an RNN-Transducer with a language model that completes partial hypotheses. The RNN-T transcribes the incomplete utterance, and the hypotheses are fed into the LM to speculate likely completions.
- **Endpoint anticipation in voice agents:** A 2026 arXiv paper (2606.13450) forecasts end-of-turn signals and runs ASR, LLM, and TTS speculatively. It reports a 505 ms average latency reduction with a 28.4% increase in speculative computation.
- **Speculative LLM generation:** A practitioner explainer describes sending partial user speech to the LLM early and holding the reply unplayed until the turn is confirmed. The mechanism is the same, but it is not a research result.
- **Anticipated-rollout precomputation:** A 2026 arXiv paper (2607.03093) for text dialogue has the model hypothesize several plausible next user replies during idle time and precompute responses for them. This is the closest match to "enumerate candidates," but it is text-based and not spoken.
- **Intent prediction:** A patent (US 10614799) describes predicting intent from a partial utterance before end-of-utterance detection, then inferring the words the user has not yet spoken.

For database-backed spoken QA specifically, a further search would be needed. The results above describe the general pattern: speculate on partial input, precompute, then confirm or discard once the utterance ends.

Spoken deltas like "no, September" or "and restaurants?" would be mapped by a tiny classifier onto that query, which is a much smaller task than full parsing, and the same state could drive a chart on screen.

I'm framing the whole idea as a "query-state duplex": the call is a continuous edit of a live typed query, not a series of turns. Acting early is cheap and reversible, since a false endpoint just means the answer gets re-bound when the user keeps talking, so the turn-taking problem partly dissolves. I'm also noting the assistant could even complete a half-finished question from its predictions, like offering "...on groceries?" after a pause.

The search didn't turn up work that matches the exact setup of a model revising its own spoken answer mid-utterance after a user correction. It did surface several closely related lines of work.

- **Self-correction in user speech is a known weak spot.** Full-Duplex-Bench-v3 tests whether voice agents can track a user who changes their mind mid-sentence and update downstream tool parameters. It reports that all systems handle surface-level disfluencies reasonably well but struggle when a user changes intent mid-utterance. Even the best model, GPT-Realtime, fails on over 40% of self-correction scenarios.
- **The cause is partly pipeline latency.** The same benchmark notes that cascaded systems commit intermediate parameters before the correction arrives, so the downstream LLM never sees the revision.
- **Interrupting to fix the agent's own errors is a new benchmark.** Model Interruption Bench (EMNLP 2026) asks whether full-duplex agents can proactively interrupt a user mid-utterance to correct a content error. This is about the agent correcting the user, not the reverse.
- **Overlap handling trades off two strategies.** Full-Duplex-Bench v1.5 describes repair-first models that yield within 300 ms but risk false triggers, and continuity-first models that maintain flow at the cost of multi-second double-talk.
- **Related interruption evaluation.** The ICASSP 2026 HumDial challenge includes a track where a model must adjust or correct its response when a user objects mid-utterance.

I didn't find a paper or system that specifically shows an LLM retracting or rewriting words it has already spoken. For that, you would likely need to search for terms like "retraction" or "barge-in" alongside "speech-to-speech."

content.content:
**Endpoint Anticipation for Low-Latency Spoken Dialogue** (Udupa, Watanabe, Schwarz, Černocký; arXiv:2606.13450, accepted at Interspeech 2026)

- **Method:** The paper argues that cascaded spoken dialogue systems are slowed by reactive turn-completion detection. It proposes Endpoint Anticipation, which forecasts end-of-turn signals in advance. The authors describe this as a shift to "proactive forecasting of end-of-turn signals."
- **What is speculated:** The model predicts endpoints up to 2.56 seconds ahead, so the LLM and TTS pipelines can start running on partial context before the user finishes speaking.
- **Models:** The core model is speech-based. It is compared against competitive VAP-based (Voice Activity Projection) baselines.
- **Results:**
  - Latency: In integration with the Unmute framework, average latency drops by 505 ms.
  - Waste: Speculative computation rises by 28.4%. The authors introduce metrics for the trade-off between realized latency reduction and computational redundancy, but the page does not report those metrics' values.
  - Accuracy: The model consistently outperforms the VAP baselines on conversational and task-oriented datasets.
- **Tools handling:** The approach is demonstrated with the Unmute framework for real-time speech-to-speech interaction. Speculative LLM and TTS execution is the mechanism that hides sequential bottlenecks.
- **Limitations:** The page contains only the abstract and metadata, so I can't confirm architecture details, datasets, model sizes, error or false-trigger analysis, or a limitations section. The abstract does not describe failure cases, and the waste cost is given only as a single percentage.

content.content:
**Problem:** Full-duplex evaluation usually asks whether a voice agent keeps speaking or stops. The authors argue this binary misses a third response that humans use often: continuing to speak while incorporating what the listener just said, such as a missing word, a correction, or a clarification.

**What "adapt" means:** The paper defines adaptation as "in-turn adaptation," which includes both acknowledgment and content revision. The speaker keeps the turn going and changes or extends what it is saying in response to the listener's overlapping contribution. The abstract doesn't describe the mechanism in detail, so it's unclear from this page how an agent would revise mid-utterance.

**Method and models:**
- The authors introduce **Duplex Cue**, an evaluation framework. It separates listener intent (backchannel, collaboration, or interruption) from speaker behavior (continue unchanged, adapt, or yield).
- In a single-model case study, they used 300 human-confirmed cues from unscripted English conversations.
- They compared recorded human responses with continuations from **PersonaPlex**, generated while replaying the listener's audio.
- They kept 208 pairs where the speaker was active at cue onset and a response was scorable in both conditions.

**Tools/data grounding:** The evaluation is grounded in recorded human conversation data. The abstract mentions no external tools or retrieval.

**Results (collaborative pairs, n=66):**
- Recorded human speakers adapted in 68.2% of cases.
- PersonaPlex adapted in 34.8%, continued unchanged in 42.4%, and yielded in 22.7%.

**Limitations:**
- This summary is based only on the abstract and metadata page, not the full paper, so details on scoring, the other intent categories, and the model's architecture are unavailable.
- The study is a single-model case study, so the findings may not generalize to other full-duplex systems.
- Data is English-only, and the key comparison rests on 66 collaborative pairs.
- Only 208 of the 300 cues were retained for analysis.

## 5. Second research round (2026-11-15): what is already taken, what is open

Checked each idea from section 3 against the literature. Most of them have close neighbours:

| Idea | Already published | Still open |
|---|---|---|
| Listen with knowledge of own speech | Textual Echo Cancellation (Google 2020, arXiv 2008.06006) uses the TTS text as echo reference; implicit AEC (Amazon, arXiv 2111.10639) feeds the reference into the classifier; Self-Listening (arXiv 2609.05592); PACE | Doing it in a sub-MB head on a 17 MB recogniser on CPU |
| Tiny turn/state head on recogniser features | Voice-Light adapter (183K weights, failed), SoulX-Duplug (0.6B LLM, GPU, user audio only), FSM tapes (arXiv 2609.03321) | Small and CPU, with the playback as input |
| Start work before the sentence ends | Personalized Predictive ASR (Amazon, Interspeech 2023, arXiv 2305.13794) predicts the full utterance and prefetches; Speculative Speech Recognition (arXiv 2407.04641); Endpoint Anticipation (arXiv 2606.13450, 505 ms saved, 28% extra compute); Voice-Light | Tools with read/write safety |
| Local fast path learned from a big model | Distil Labs banking voice assistant (0.35-0.6B tool-calling model distilled offline, about 40 ms); Agentic Plan Caching (NeurIPS 2025); AgenticCache (MLSys 2026, background validator); Google patent on distilling from observed query patterns | Learning online from the owner's own calls with background checking |
| Think between calls | Sleep-time Compute (arXiv 2504.13171); "Don't Wait to Reply" (arXiv 2607.03093) | Voice, personal data, validity tied to data version |
| Per-user turn-taking | Bandit endpointing (arXiv 2303.13407), speaker-embedding endpointing (SLT 2021) | On-device learning from the owner's interruptions |
| Check audio before it plays | Only offline round-trip testing (AssemblyAI guide and others) | Live guard: nothing found |

The open gap that matters most:
- Full-Duplex-Bench v3: when the user changes their mind mid-sentence, even the best system (GPT-Realtime) fails over 40% of the time; cascades commit parameters before the correction arrives.
- "Continue, Adapt, or Yield" (arXiv 2609.13117): in real conversations people keep talking and fold in the listener's correction 68% of the time; PersonaPlex does so 35%. It is an evaluation paper only. No system was found that changes a data-grounded answer mid-sentence.
- Older academic lineage to credit: incremental dialogue systems with revisable units and self-repair (Skantze and Schlangen; Skantze and Hjalmarsson 2010), and "revise" operations on dialogue programs (SMCalFlow dataflow). Toy domains, turn-based or pre-LLM.

Direction chosen for the next phase (proposal, not built): **live-query duplex**. The call is treated as continuous editing of one typed finance query (metric, category, period, account, comparison) that deterministic Moneo code answers in milliseconds. Tiny local models turn each new word, including words spoken over the assistant, into an edit of that query; speech is a view of the query that can be re-bound mid-sentence. The big model works between calls and on misses.

## 6. Sources

content.text:
I checked my earlier ideas against the literature, and most are already published. The one I found nothing like, and the one I'd build the research around, is a call where you can correct Moneo mid-sentence and it changes its answer without stopping.

## What's already taken

| My earlier idea | Who did it |
|---|---|
| Listen while knowing your own speech | Google 2020 (uses the TTS text to cancel echo), Amazon 2021, a "self-listening" paper from Sept 2026 |
| Start work before the sentence ends | Amazon 2023 (predicts the rest of the sentence and prefetches), two 2024 papers and two 2026 ones |
| Tiny local model taught by a big one | Distil Labs has a local banking voice assistant doing this |
| Think between calls | "Sleep-time compute" (2025) |
| Turn-taking that adapts to one person | Papers from 2021 and 2023 |

Checking audio before it plays is the only one I found nowhere as a live guard, but it is a feature, not a thesis.

## The gap nobody has filled

- When a user changes their mind mid-sentence, even the best system (OpenAI's) gets it wrong over 40% of the time, per Full-Duplex-Bench v3.
- In real conversations people keep talking and fold in the other person's correction 68% of the time. A leading open model does it 35% of the time (a Sept 2026 paper, which only measures this).
- I found no system that changes a real, data-backed answer mid-sentence.

## The options

1. **Better ears:** a tiny model that separates you from Moneo's own voice. Needed, but not new.
2. **Guess the sentence ending:** crowded field, and I measured only about 0.3 s gained.
3. **Answers prepared between calls:** useful, but the idea exists.
4. **Local fast path taught by the big model:** very useful, exists in parts.
5. **Live-query call:** new, and it uses 1, 3 and 4 as its engine.
6. **Our own tiny speech-to-speech model:** biggest effort, and the least different from Moshi.

## My pick: option 5, the live-query call

Stop treating a call as turns. Treat it as the two of you editing one question together.

- **One typed question.** Every money question becomes a small structured query: what, which category, which period, which account, compared to what. Moneo's own code answers it in milliseconds, so numbers come from code, never from a model.
- **Every word is an edit.** Tiny local models turn each new word into a change to that query, including words you say while Moneo is talking.
- **Speech follows the query.** You say "no, September" while it is speaking and it carries on: "…September was 265."
- **Mistakes get cheap.** Starting too early no longer matters much, because the answer just re-binds when you keep talking. That eases the pause problem I couldn't fix.
- **The big model moves off the call.** It prepares between calls, teaches the small models, and handles the unusual questions.

If it works, the demo is exact answers in about 0.3 s that you can steer while it talks, on a laptop CPU. Open benchmarks to score it already exist. The neighbouring ideas are older academic systems on toy tasks and turn-based "revise" operations, which the paper would credit.

Nothing is built yet; this round was reading only. The log is updated with every paper I checked.
